iGEM Jamboree Competition More  Sign In  Community Technology Responsibility Startups Leagues Projects On this page Rules and Policies iGEM Competition teams must follow all of the rules and policies listed on this page.  This is a requirement for participating in the iGEM Competition. Every team PI, student team member, instructor, and advisor on the team roster is expected to read this page. It is unacceptable to claim you broke the rules and/or policies because you were unaware of them.  Failure to follow the rules and policies listed below may result in serious consequences for your team, up to and including ineligibility for medals and/or awards, disqualification from the competition, and banning and suspension from participation in iGEM.  Conduct in the iGEM Competition is overseen by two committees of external experts: the Safety & Security Committee and the Responsible Conduct Committee. These two committees work closely together throughout the year when violations of the rules and/or policies are reported.  Safety & Security Committee  The iGEM Safety & Security Committee is a group of experts in biosafety, biosecurity, and risk assessment. Its members come from diverse areas of industry, academia, and government.  The committee helps create iGEM's safety & security program and gives expert advice on potential safety & security issues in the competition.  Responsible Conduct Committee  The iGEM Responsible Conduct Committee (RCC) is an external panel of experts who deal with all issues related to conduct in the competition. Our RCC members collectively have over 50 years of experience in the iGEM competition and are well versed in conduct and behavior related issues.  The role of the Responsible Conduct Committee is to ensure a high standard of conduct on the part of all iGEM participants and to address issues of inappropriate behavior in iGEM.  The Safety & Security Committee at the 2023 Grand Jamboree in Paris. In the back row, from left to right: Sam Evans, Piers Millett, Georgie Sorensen, Chris Isaac, Yorgo El Moubayed. In the front row: Kathryn Millett, Svenja Vinke, Tessa Alexanian, Alonso Flores (iGEM HQ Safety & Security Program Officer). Several other committee members, though not pictured, also play an integral role in ensuring that teams are working safely. The Responsible Conduct Committee at the 2023 Grand Jamboree in Paris. From left to right: Peter Carr (co-chair), King Chow, Piers Millett, Christopher French (chair), Lucas Boldrini (iGEM HQ Liaison), Christopher Workman, Dorothy Zhang (iGEM HQ). Karmella Haynes is also in the picture, participating virtually. Not pictured: Genya Dana. Rules of Conduct  All members of our community are expected to abide by our Rules of Conduct. These rules apply to everyone involved in iGEM, including the iGEM Competition and League teams (which includes team members, instructors, advisors, and PIs), judges, committee(s) and network members, community participants, and iGEM Headquarters staff.  Failure to follow the Rules of Conduct will be brought to the attention of the Responsible Conduct Committee and they will determine what, if any, action will be taken.  1. Uphold iGEM's Values  Every iGEM participant is expected to uphold iGEM’s values at all times, which include: integrity, good sportsmanship, respect, honesty, celebration, cooperation, effort, and excellence. iGEMers are ambassadors for the global synthetic biology community; teams and projects may have a large impact beyond the competition.  2. Be Intellectually Honest  Teams should describe their accomplishments accurately and honestly. The current year's team members should not take credit for the work of other researchers, even if those researchers were previous members of your institution's iGEM team. This also includes not intentionally misrepresenting results, and not making unsubstantiated claims about your work.  We treat any and all failure to uphold intellectual honesty by anyone associated with a team, including students, advisors, or faculty members, as a form of cheating.  Teams should use the Project Attribution page on their wiki to clearly state who conducted any and all work for the project. If an experiment, tool development, or other part of the project was done by someone who is not currently a member of your team, obtain that person's permission to include their work, and clearly describe their contribution in Project Attribution. If their work was included in a public document or digital medium (publication, website, iGEM Wiki, etc.) clearly cite their work. Teams should also note which parts of the project were derived from the scientific literature throughout their project documentation.  Failure to correctly cite work from others who are not current official team members will be considered a form of plagiarism, which is a form of cheating.  3. Treat Everyone with Respect  All iGEM participants are expected to treat everyone with respect. You must recognize and consider the perspectives, experiences, and dignity of others. You must be sensitive to the inherent worth of all human beings and the consideration that they are due. This includes, but is not limited to, student team members, PIs, instructors, advisors, other teams, judges, community members, Headquarters staff, and members of the public.  4. Consider Cultural Context  We want every member of our community to feel a sense of belonging, and we know that teams (and iGEM HQ) cannot perfectly anticipate what is needed to create a positive shared environment for iGEM’s diverse, global participants. Your online materials and videos may be unintentionally seen as offensive or disrespectful by some members of our community. Equally, you may find materials or videos offensive. In either case, members of our community should consider how cultural contexts differ around the world. When we are notified of these issues, we may ask you to add disclaimers to your materials or revise the content.  Safety Rules  The Safety & Security Committee reviews any misconduct reported as it pertains to the Safety Rule and Safety Policies below and determines what, if any, action will be taken.  Teams must fill in the Safety Form to provide information on any risks from their project and steps taken to manage those risks. Hazardous organisms, parts or activities: Teams must submit additional Check-In Forms and get approval by the Safety & Security Committee BEFORE beginning experiments for projects involving parts, organisms, or activities that are not on the White List. Refer to the White List Policy. If considering the use of gene drives within a project, teams will need to refer to the Gene Drives Policy. If planning to use new antimicrobial resistance factors, or those new to a chassis, or their institution, teams will need to refer to the Anti-Microbial Resistance Policy. If intending to use parts from, or live SARS-CoV-2, teams will need to refer to the SARS-CoV-2 Policy. Animal Use Forms: Teams must get permission from the Safety & Security Committee BEFORE beginning experiments for projects involving vertebrates and some invertebrates. This includes the use of live or dead animals, and animal samples such as organs, tissues, blood, saliva, or other bodily fluids. Refer to the Animal Use Policy. Failure to meet this requirement has been the most common reason for disqualification of iGEM teams. The team’s Primary PI, Secondary PI, or Instructor must sign the Safety Form and any Animal Use Form the team submits. Teams must meet all safety & security deadlines, including those given in email communications from the Safety & Security Committee. Teams must follow all relevant international, regional, national, local or institutional laws, rules, regulations, or policies, including national or institutional biosafety and biosecurity rules applicable to the each team. For teams conducting any experiment with human subjects (including non-invasive experiments, such as surveys), teams must comply with all rules governing experiments with human subjects. Refer to the Human Experimentation Policy and Human Subjects Research Policy. Teams must work in the biosafety level appropriate for their project. If a project involves organisms and parts that can be used safely in a BSL1 lab, the team should not work at higher containment levels. If this is not possible, an explanation must be provided in the Safety Form. Teams cannot conduct work with Risk Group 3 or 4 organisms, parts from a Risk Group 4 organism, or work in a Safety Level 3 or 4 laboratory. This includes work with large volumes or high concentrations of SARS-CoV-2, whether isolated virus, or human, animal, or environmental samples likely to contain it. Teams cannot release or deploy their project outside of the laboratory at any time during the Competition or at the Grand Jamboree. Refer to the Release Beyond Containment Policy. Teams cannot test their project on or in human subjects. Testing your product on humans (including yourselves) is strictly prohibited. Refer to the Human Experimentation Policy. Safety Policies  Safety Policies provide further clarification on the use of specific technologies in the iGEM Competition. For a more detailed explanation of these policies, and information about how to request permission to use specific technologies, please visit the Safety Policies Introduction. Teams are responsible for checking the Policies page prior to beginning any work, as the policies may be updated throughout the iGEM Competition.   Release Beyond Containment: You cannot release or deploy any genetically modified organisms outside the lab. You must check in before bringing any product of synthetic biology outside of the lab. Review this policy.  White List: You must check in before beginning experiments with any organism, part, or activity that is not on the White List. Review this policy.  Human Experimentation: Testing your project on humans (including yourselves) is strictly prohibited. You must check in before beginning any laboratory experiments involving humans or human samples (including but not limited to blood, DNA, other bodily specimens, and health or psychological outcomes). Review this policy.  Animal Use: You must check in before beginning any experiments involving animals or animal samples. This includes vertebrates (e.g. rats, mice, guinea pigs, hamsters, amphibians, and fishes) and higher order invertebrates (e.g. cuttlefish, octopus, squid, lobster, bees, or American or German cockroaches). Review this policy.  Human Subjects Research: All human subjects research (e.g. surveys, interviews, public engagement) you carry out must be done in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, as well as any institutional rules or guidance. Review this policy.  Gene Drives: Gene drives are not allowed in iGEM projects without a special exception from the Safety & Security Committee. Review this policy.  Antimicrobial Resistance: You must check in before beginning experiments likely to change the risk posed by antimicrobial resistance (e.g. by using novel resistance factors, adding known factors into new organisms, or using resistance factors not previously used in your facility). Review this policy.  SARS-CoV-2: Any work using live SARS-CoV-2 virus (the causative agent of COVID-19) must follow World Health Organization (WHO) guidance, in addition to all local and institutional rules. WHO guidance may be stricter than local safety rules. You must check in before beginning experiments with live SARS-CoV-2 or parts from SARS-CoV-2 . Review this policy.  Environmental Samples: As long as parts or organisms are not isolated from them, samples from the environment, the food industry, or other non-traditional suppliers may be used in your experiments. You must check in before using any parts organisms obtained from outside the lab or from non-traditional suppliers. Review this policy. Communications Policies  These policies are for any material you make as part of your project, including promotional materials, videos, social media posts, wiki pages, and other materials.  Be honest and accurate: You should represent your project and results both honestly and accurately. This is especially important when describing your project's likelihood of solving real world problems. Recognize that many people are eager for hope and it can be tempting to over-promise. An iGEM team is not expected to scale their project into a regional or national solution during one season of the competition. Be yourself: No team member should pretend to have a disability, medical condition, cultural affiliation, or racial identity that they do not have in real life. This may happen with the best of intentions, but comes with a real risk of spreading stereotypes or otherwise failing to treat everyone with respect. No country flags: Country flags are not allowed to be displayed in your videos or promotional materials. We know many teams are proud of the place they come from. However, iGEM is an international competition and we nuture a scientific community of mutual trust and respect, and country flags can unfortunately bring international tensions into what we want to be a collaborative, celebratory environment. Don't include disturbing imagery: We know you may be addressing serious and upsetting issues, but we ask that you consider whether disturbing imagery is truly necessary. Videos containing scenes of violence, death, drug use, or other potentially disturbing content must have warnings added or be removed from iGEM’s platforms. Teams cannot use any copyrighted materials: Copyrighted images and other materials are not permitted on the iGEM wiki. You may use materials that are appropriately licensed for reuse, such as open-source code or Creative Commons licensed images. If you use copyrighted materials, we reserve the right to remove the content at will. Teams must host all online content on iGEM servers: All team pages, images, documents and code must be hosted on the iGEM servers. Load your CSS, Javascript, or Bootstrap files into the iGEM server, either directly into your page or using templates. Do not link to scripts or stylesheets that are hosted on other servers. We preserve all iGEM content on our own servers so future teams can learn from what you have done. When you store content on your own sites or servers, links might become broken, sites might go down, and information will be lost. Hosting content outside of the iGEM servers is a form of cheating and may result in no medal. Anti-Harassment Policy  The iGEM Foundation strictly prohibits harassment of any kind. For the purposes of this policy, harassment may include, but is not limited to, the following:  any form of verbal, physical, and/or sexual harassment any conduct intended to threaten, intimidate, or coerce another individual uninvited physical contact unwelcome attention intimidation, stalking, or following any discriminatory acts related to age, race, gender, or sexual orientation, status, etc. advocating for or encouraging any of the above behaviors  Harassment can be verbal or nonverbal, and includes offensive comments and gestures, and the distribution, display, and/or discussion of offensive material. This includes harassment during online events and activities and/or over social media as well as during any in person events.  iGEM Foundation staff will take appropriate and immediate action in response to complaints or knowledge of violations of this policy. During in-person events like the the Grand Jamboree or other iGEM-hosted events, this action may include, but is not limited to, the offender’s immediate ejection from the premises and disqualification of their team from the competition.  The Responsible Conduct Committee reviews all reports or complaints of harassment and determines what, if any, action will be taken.  Possible Consequences What happens if a team or individual violates any of the rules or policies listed above?  If a potential violation of the rules and/or policies listed on this page, or other misconduct issue is reported, the Responsible Conduct Committee and/or Safety & Security Committee will review the case and determine what consequences, if any, the team and/or participant will face for failing to follow these rules and policies.  For serious violations, here are some of the possible consequences: Full disqualification: A team is disqualified from the competition. The team is unable to receive any awards or medals, and their wiki may be removed from the iGEM website. Partial disqualification: A part of a team’s project is disqualified. Judges are asked to proceed as if the team had not done that experiment or activity. The team may be asked to edit and/or remove sections of their wiki following the Grand Jamboree. Ineligibility for special prizes: A team is declared ineligible for certain special prizes, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ineligibility for medals: A team is declared ineligible for medals, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ban from future involvement in iGEM: In the most extreme cases, individuals and/or institutions may be banned from participating in future competitions. For minor violations, here are some of the possible consequences: Cease actions and adjust project plans: If minimal harm has occurred, it may be sufficient for a team to cease the potentially harmful actions, and change their planned experiment(s) and/or design(s). There may also be a discussion or other communication with guidance from the relevant committee. Add disclaimers or additional context: One result of an investigation into a complaint of violation of iGEM rules could be that a team may be asked to update wiki pages, presentations, videos, or other materials to clarify the situation. Add content warnings or revise materials: Content that is acceptable in a local context may have a negative impact on some members of iGEM’s diverse, global community. In such cases, teams may be asked to add content warnings and/or to revise their materials to be more globally appropriate. Materials include the team wiki, videos, and any other content the team may create. What actions would violate the Rules and Policies?  Below you'll find some examples of situations that would violate the Rules and Policies outlined above. If any scenario like these examples came to our attention, it would be investigated by either the Safety & Security or Responsible Conduct Committee. Please note that these are hypothetical situations. These are not a description of the actions of any specific team.  Unauthorized Animal Use  Scenario: A team wants to test their siRNA therapeutic on cancer cells. They don’t have access to a cancer cell line, but another lab at their institution offers the team some tissue samples from mice that they will be euthanizing. Since the team is not experimenting on live animals, they do not plan to submit an Animal Use Form to iGEM. These two committees work closely together throughout the year when violations of the rules and/or policies are reported. Its members come from diverse areas of industry, academia, and government.  The committee helps create iGEM's safety & security program and gives expert advice on potential safety & security issues in the competition.  Responsible Conduct Committee  The iGEM Responsible Conduct Committee (RCC) is an external panel of experts who deal with all issues related to conduct in the competition. Our RCC members collectively have over 50 years of experience in the iGEM competition and are well versed in conduct and behavior related issues.  The role of the Responsible Conduct Committee is to ensure a high standard of conduct on the part of all iGEM participants and to address issues of inappropriate behavior in iGEM. Karmella Haynes is also in the picture, participating virtually. Not pictured: Genya Dana. Rules of Conduct  All members of our community are expected to abide by our Rules of Conduct. These rules apply to everyone involved in iGEM, including the iGEM Competition and League teams (which includes team members, instructors, advisors, and PIs), judges, committee(s) and network members, community participants, and iGEM Headquarters staff.  Failure to follow the Rules of Conduct will be brought to the attention of the Responsible Conduct Committee and they will determine what, if any, action will be taken.  1. Uphold iGEM's Values  Every iGEM participant is expected to uphold iGEM’s values at all times, which include: integrity, good sportsmanship, respect, honesty, celebration, cooperation, effort, and excellence. iGEMers are ambassadors for the global synthetic biology community; teams and projects may have a large impact beyond the competition.  2. Be Intellectually Honest  Teams should describe their accomplishments accurately and honestly. The current year's team members should not take credit for the work of other researchers, even if those researchers were previous members of your institution's iGEM team. This also includes not intentionally misrepresenting results, and not making unsubstantiated claims about your work.  We treat any and all failure to uphold intellectual honesty by anyone associated with a team, including students, advisors, or faculty members, as a form of cheating.  Teams should use the Project Attribution page on their wiki to clearly state who conducted any and all work for the project. If an experiment, tool development, or other part of the project was done by someone who is not currently a member of your team, obtain that person's permission to include their work, and clearly describe their contribution in Project Attribution. If their work was included in a public document or digital medium (publication, website, iGEM Wiki, etc.) clearly cite their work. Teams should also note which parts of the project were derived from the scientific literature throughout their project documentation.  Failure to correctly cite work from others who are not current official team members will be considered a form of plagiarism, which is a form of cheating.  3. Treat Everyone with Respect  All iGEM participants are expected to treat everyone with respect. You must recognize and consider the perspectives, experiences, and dignity of others. You must be sensitive to the inherent worth of all human beings and the consideration that they are due. This includes, but is not limited to, student team members, PIs, instructors, advisors, other teams, judges, community members, Headquarters staff, and members of the public.  4. Consider Cultural Context  We want every member of our community to feel a sense of belonging, and we know that teams (and iGEM HQ) cannot perfectly anticipate what is needed to create a positive shared environment for iGEM’s diverse, global participants. Your online materials and videos may be unintentionally seen as offensive or disrespectful by some members of our community. Equally, you may find materials or videos offensive. In either case, members of our community should consider how cultural contexts differ around the world. When we are notified of these issues, we may ask you to add disclaimers to your materials or revise the content.  Safety Rules  The Safety & Security Committee reviews any misconduct reported as it pertains to the Safety Rule and Safety Policies below and determines what, if any, action will be taken.  Teams must fill in the Safety Form to provide information on any risks from their project and steps taken to manage those risks. Hazardous organisms, parts or activities: Teams must submit additional Check-In Forms and get approval by the Safety & Security Committee BEFORE beginning experiments for projects involving parts, organisms, or activities that are not on the White List. Refer to the White List Policy. If considering the use of gene drives within a project, teams will need to refer to the Gene Drives Policy. If planning to use new antimicrobial resistance factors, or those new to a chassis, or their institution, teams will need to refer to the Anti-Microbial Resistance Policy. If intending to use parts from, or live SARS-CoV-2, teams will need to refer to the SARS-CoV-2 Policy. Animal Use Forms: Teams must get permission from the Safety & Security Committee BEFORE beginning experiments for projects involving vertebrates and some invertebrates. This includes the use of live or dead animals, and animal samples such as organs, tissues, blood, saliva, or other bodily fluids. Refer to the Animal Use Policy. Failure to meet this requirement has been the most common reason for disqualification of iGEM teams. The team’s Primary PI, Secondary PI, or Instructor must sign the Safety Form and any Animal Use Form the team submits. Teams must meet all safety & security deadlines, including those given in email communications from the Safety & Security Committee. Teams must follow all relevant international, regional, national, local or institutional laws, rules, regulations, or policies, including national or institutional biosafety and biosecurity rules applicable to the each team. For teams conducting any experiment with human subjects (including non-invasive experiments, such as surveys), teams must comply with all rules governing experiments with human subjects. Refer to the Human Experimentation Policy and Human Subjects Research Policy. Teams must work in the biosafety level appropriate for their project. If a project involves organisms and parts that can be used safely in a BSL1 lab, the team should not work at higher containment levels. If this is not possible, an explanation must be provided in the Safety Form. Teams cannot conduct work with Risk Group 3 or 4 organisms, parts from a Risk Group 4 organism, or work in a Safety Level 3 or 4 laboratory. This includes work with large volumes or high concentrations of SARS-CoV-2, whether isolated virus, or human, animal, or environmental samples likely to contain it. Teams cannot release or deploy their project outside of the laboratory at any time during the Competition or at the Grand Jamboree. Refer to the Release Beyond Containment Policy. Teams cannot test their project on or in human subjects. Testing your product on humans (including yourselves) is strictly prohibited. Refer to the Human Experimentation Policy. Safety Policies  Safety Policies provide further clarification on the use of specific technologies in the iGEM Competition. For a more detailed explanation of these policies, and information about how to request permission to use specific technologies, please visit the Safety Policies Introduction. Teams are responsible for checking the Policies page prior to beginning any work, as the policies may be updated throughout the iGEM Competition.   Release Beyond Containment: You cannot release or deploy any genetically modified organisms outside the lab. You must check in before bringing any product of synthetic biology outside of the lab. Review this policy.  White List: You must check in before beginning experiments with any organism, part, or activity that is not on the White List. Review this policy.  Human Experimentation: Testing your project on humans (including yourselves) is strictly prohibited. You must check in before beginning any laboratory experiments involving humans or human samples (including but not limited to blood, DNA, other bodily specimens, and health or psychological outcomes). Review this policy.  Animal Use: You must check in before beginning any experiments involving animals or animal samples. This includes vertebrates (e.g. rats, mice, guinea pigs, hamsters, amphibians, and fishes) and higher order invertebrates (e.g. cuttlefish, octopus, squid, lobster, bees, or American or German cockroaches). Review this policy.  Human Subjects Research: All human subjects research (e.g. surveys, interviews, public engagement) you carry out must be done in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, as well as any institutional rules or guidance. Review this policy.  Gene Drives: Gene drives are not allowed in iGEM projects without a special exception from the Safety & Security Committee. Review this policy.  Antimicrobial Resistance: You must check in before beginning experiments likely to change the risk posed by antimicrobial resistance (e.g. by using novel resistance factors, adding known factors into new organisms, or using resistance factors not previously used in your facility). Review this policy.  SARS-CoV-2: Any work using live SARS-CoV-2 virus (the causative agent of COVID-19) must follow World Health Organization (WHO) guidance, in addition to all local and institutional rules. WHO guidance may be stricter than local safety rules. You must check in before beginning experiments with live SARS-CoV-2 or parts from SARS-CoV-2 . Review this policy.  Environmental Samples: As long as parts or organisms are not isolated from them, samples from the environment, the food industry, or other non-traditional suppliers may be used in your experiments. You must check in before using any parts organisms obtained from outside the lab or from non-traditional suppliers. Review this policy. Communications Policies  These policies are for any material you make as part of your project, including promotional materials, videos, social media posts, wiki pages, and other materials.  Be honest and accurate: You should represent your project and results both honestly and accurately. This is especially important when describing your project's likelihood of solving real world problems. Recognize that many people are eager for hope and it can be tempting to over-promise. An iGEM team is not expected to scale their project into a regional or national solution during one season of the competition. Be yourself: No team member should pretend to have a disability, medical condition, cultural affiliation, or racial identity that they do not have in real life. This may happen with the best of intentions, but comes with a real risk of spreading stereotypes or otherwise failing to treat everyone with respect. No country flags: Country flags are not allowed to be displayed in your videos or promotional materials. We know many teams are proud of the place they come from. However, iGEM is an international competition and we nuture a scientific community of mutual trust and respect, and country flags can unfortunately bring international tensions into what we want to be a collaborative, celebratory environment. Don't include disturbing imagery: We know you may be addressing serious and upsetting issues, but we ask that you consider whether disturbing imagery is truly necessary. Videos containing scenes of violence, death, drug use, or other potentially disturbing content must have warnings added or be removed from iGEM’s platforms. Teams cannot use any copyrighted materials: Copyrighted images and other materials are not permitted on the iGEM wiki. You may use materials that are appropriately licensed for reuse, such as open-source code or Creative Commons licensed images. If you use copyrighted materials, we reserve the right to remove the content at will. Teams must host all online content on iGEM servers: All team pages, images, documents and code must be hosted on the iGEM servers. Load your CSS, Javascript, or Bootstrap files into the iGEM server, either directly into your page or using templates. Do not link to scripts or stylesheets that are hosted on other servers. We preserve all iGEM content on our own servers so future teams can learn from what you have done. When you store content on your own sites or servers, links might become broken, sites might go down, and information will be lost. Hosting content outside of the iGEM servers is a form of cheating and may result in no medal. Anti-Harassment Policy  The iGEM Foundation strictly prohibits harassment of any kind. For the purposes of this policy, harassment may include, but is not limited to, the following:  any form of verbal, physical, and/or sexual harassment any conduct intended to threaten, intimidate, or coerce another individual uninvited physical contact unwelcome attention intimidation, stalking, or following any discriminatory acts related to age, race, gender, or sexual orientation, status, etc. advocating for or encouraging any of the above behaviors  Harassment can be verbal or nonverbal, and includes offensive comments and gestures, and the distribution, display, and/or discussion of offensive material. This includes harassment during online events and activities and/or over social media as well as during any in person events.  iGEM Foundation staff will take appropriate and immediate action in response to complaints or knowledge of violations of this policy. During in-person events like the the Grand Jamboree or other iGEM-hosted events, this action may include, but is not limited to, the offender’s immediate ejection from the premises and disqualification of their team from the competition.  The Responsible Conduct Committee reviews all reports or complaints of harassment and determines what, if any, action will be taken.  Possible Consequences What happens if a team or individual violates any of the rules or policies listed above?  If a potential violation of the rules and/or policies listed on this page, or other misconduct issue is reported, the Responsible Conduct Committee and/or Safety & Security Committee will review the case and determine what consequences, if any, the team and/or participant will face for failing to follow these rules and policies.  For serious violations, here are some of the possible consequences: Full disqualification: A team is disqualified from the competition. The team is unable to receive any awards or medals, and their wiki may be removed from the iGEM website. Partial disqualification: A part of a team’s project is disqualified. Judges are asked to proceed as if the team had not done that experiment or activity. The team may be asked to edit and/or remove sections of their wiki following the Grand Jamboree. Ineligibility for special prizes: A team is declared ineligible for certain special prizes, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ineligibility for medals: A team is declared ineligible for medals, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ban from future involvement in iGEM: In the most extreme cases, individuals and/or institutions may be banned from participating in future competitions. There may also be a discussion or other communication with guidance from the relevant committee. Add disclaimers or additional context: One result of an investigation into a complaint of violation of iGEM rules could be that a team may be asked to update wiki pages, presentations, videos, or other materials to clarify the situation. Add content warnings or revise materials: Content that is acceptable in a local context may have a negative impact on some members of iGEM’s diverse, global community. Review this policy.  White List: You must check in before beginning experiments with any organism, part, or activity that is not on the White List. Review this policy.  Human Experimentation: Testing your project on humans (including yourselves) is strictly prohibited. You must check in before beginning any laboratory experiments involving humans or human samples (including but not limited to blood, DNA, other bodily specimens, and health or psychological outcomes). Review this policy.  Animal Use: You must check in before beginning any experiments involving animals or animal samples. This includes vertebrates (e.g. rats, mice, guinea pigs, hamsters, amphibians, and fishes) and higher order invertebrates (e.g. cuttlefish, octopus, squid, lobster, bees, or American or German cockroaches). Review this policy.  Human Subjects Research: All human subjects research (e.g. surveys, interviews, public engagement) you carry out must be done in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, as well as any institutional rules or guidance. Review this policy.  Gene Drives: Gene drives are not allowed in iGEM projects without a special exception from the Safety & Security Committee. Review this policy.  Antimicrobial Resistance: You must check in before beginning experiments likely to change the risk posed by antimicrobial resistance (e.g. by using novel resistance factors, adding known factors into new organisms, or using resistance factors not previously used in your facility). Review this policy.  SARS-CoV-2: Any work using live SARS-CoV-2 virus (the causative agent of COVID-19) must follow World Health Organization (WHO) guidance, in addition to all local and institutional rules. WHO guidance may be stricter than local safety rules. You must check in before beginning experiments with live SARS-CoV-2 or parts from SARS-CoV-2 . Review this policy.  Environmental Samples: As long as parts or organisms are not isolated from them, samples from the environment, the food industry, or other non-traditional suppliers may be used in your experiments. You must check in before using any parts organisms obtained from outside the lab or from non-traditional suppliers. Review this policy. Communications Policies  These policies are for any material you make as part of your project, including promotional materials, videos, social media posts, wiki pages, and other materials.  Be honest and accurate: You should represent your project and results both honestly and accurately. This is especially important when describing your project's likelihood of solving real world problems. Recognize that many people are eager for hope and it can be tempting to over-promise. An iGEM team is not expected to scale their project into a regional or national solution during one season of the competition. Be yourself: No team member should pretend to have a disability, medical condition, cultural affiliation, or racial identity that they do not have in real life. This may happen with the best of intentions, but comes with a real risk of spreading stereotypes or otherwise failing to treat everyone with respect. No country flags: Country flags are not allowed to be displayed in your videos or promotional materials. We know many teams are proud of the place they come from. However, iGEM is an international competition and we nuture a scientific community of mutual trust and respect, and country flags can unfortunately bring international tensions into what we want to be a collaborative, celebratory environment. Don't include disturbing imagery: We know you may be addressing serious and upsetting issues, but we ask that you consider whether disturbing imagery is truly necessary. Videos containing scenes of violence, death, drug use, or other potentially disturbing content must have warnings added or be removed from iGEM’s platforms. Teams cannot use any copyrighted materials: Copyrighted images and other materials are not permitted on the iGEM wiki. You may use materials that are appropriately licensed for reuse, such as open-source code or Creative Commons licensed images. If you use copyrighted materials, we reserve the right to remove the content at will. Teams must host all online content on iGEM servers: All team pages, images, documents and code must be hosted on the iGEM servers. Load your CSS, Javascript, or Bootstrap files into the iGEM server, either directly into your page or using templates. Do not link to scripts or stylesheets that are hosted on other servers. We preserve all iGEM content on our own servers so future teams can learn from what you have done. When you store content on your own sites or servers, links might become broken, sites might go down, and information will be lost. Hosting content outside of the iGEM servers is a form of cheating and may result in no medal. Anti-Harassment Policy  The iGEM Foundation strictly prohibits harassment of any kind. For the purposes of this policy, harassment may include, but is not limited to, the following:  any form of verbal, physical, and/or sexual harassment any conduct intended to threaten, intimidate, or coerce another individual uninvited physical contact unwelcome attention intimidation, stalking, or following any discriminatory acts related to age, race, gender, or sexual orientation, status, etc. advocating for or encouraging any of the above behaviors  Harassment can be verbal or nonverbal, and includes offensive comments and gestures, and the distribution, display, and/or discussion of offensive material. This includes harassment during online events and activities and/or over social media as well as during any in person events.  iGEM Foundation staff will take appropriate and immediate action in response to complaints or knowledge of violations of this policy. During in-person events like the the Grand Jamboree or other iGEM-hosted events, this action may include, but is not limited to, the offender’s immediate ejection from the premises and disqualification of their team from the competition.  The Responsible Conduct Committee reviews all reports or complaints of harassment and determines what, if any, action will be taken.  Possible Consequences What happens if a team or individual violates any of the rules or policies listed above?  If a potential violation of the rules and/or policies listed on this page, or other misconduct issue is reported, the Responsible Conduct Committee and/or Safety & Security Committee will review the case and determine what consequences, if any, the team and/or participant will face for failing to follow these rules and policies.  For serious violations, here are some of the possible consequences: Full disqualification: A team is disqualified from the competition. The team is unable to receive any awards or medals, and their wiki may be removed from the iGEM website. Partial disqualification: A part of a team’s project is disqualified. Judges are asked to proceed as if the team had not done that experiment or activity. The team may be asked to edit and/or remove sections of their wiki following the Grand Jamboree. Ineligibility for special prizes: A team is declared ineligible for certain special prizes, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ineligibility for medals: A team is declared ineligible for medals, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ban from future involvement in iGEM: In the most extreme cases, individuals and/or institutions may be banned from participating in future competitions. For minor violations, here are some of the possible consequences: Cease actions and adjust project plans: If minimal harm has occurred, it may be sufficient for a team to cease the potentially harmful actions, and change their planned experiment(s) and/or design(s). There may also be a discussion or other communication with guidance from the relevant committee. Add disclaimers or additional context: One result of an investigation into a complaint of violation of iGEM rules could be that a team may be asked to update wiki pages, presentations, videos, or other materials to clarify the situation. Add content warnings or revise materials: Content that is acceptable in a local context may have a negative impact on some members of iGEM’s diverse, global community. In such cases, teams may be asked to add content warnings and/or to revise their materials to be more globally appropriate. Materials include the team wiki, videos, and any other content the team may create. What actions would violate the Rules and Policies?  Below you'll find some examples of situations that would violate the Rules and Policies outlined above. If any scenario like these examples came to our attention, it would be investigated by either the Safety & Security or Responsible Conduct Committee. Please note that these are hypothetical situations. These are not a description of the actions of any specific team.  Unauthorized Animal Use  Scenario: A team wants to test their siRNA therapeutic on cancer cells. They don’t have access to a cancer cell line, but another lab at their institution offers the team some tissue samples from mice that they will be euthanizing. Since the team is not experimenting on live animals, they do not plan to submit an Animal Use Form to iGEM.  Rule or Policy violated: Animal Use Policy  Consequences: When judges learn about these experiments, they ask the Safety & Security Committee whether the team received approval for their animal use work. Since the team did not receive prior approval to use parts of animals, the Safety & Security Committee recommends that the team be disqualified.  Dishonest Attribution  Scenario: A team takes credit for the work of others. The team takes the results of another team (current or previous) or research group and presents that work as their own. (Note: This should not be confused with two teams that simply happen to be working on similar projects.)  Rule or Policy violated: Be Intellectually Honest  Consequences: Possible consequences could include being disqualified from receiving medals and/or awards (if before the Jamboree) or even taking away an award (if a decision can only be made after the Jamboree). iGEM takes honesty and attribution very seriously.  Judge Harassment  Scenario: Some members of a team are unhappy with the judging results and decide to take that frustration out on the judges. They send emails to the judges insulting and threatening them.  Rule or Policy violated: Treat Everyone With Respect and the Anti-Harassment Policy  Consequences: Consequences could include a team being stripped of awards and individuals banned from future involvement in iGEM. It could also result in an institution being banned from participating in future competitions for a set number of years or indefinitely. In the most extreme cases, matters would be referred to the appropriate legal authorities.  Stereotyping and Over-Promising  Scenario: A team’s promotional video includes scenes where they pretend to experience a serious medical problem. A judge flags the exaggerated way the team acted out the medical problem, including a scene which shows someone falling into a coma, while a voiceover announces that this condition would not happen if they use the team’s engineered microbiome solution.  Rule or Policy violated: Treat Everyone with Respect and the Communication Policies “Be honest and accurate" and “Be yourself”  Consequences: The RCC reaches out to make sure that the team intended for the video to be respectful, and has engaged responsibly with people who have the medical condition they are portraying during their project. As long as the discussion does not reveal other issues, the only change would be the addition of a content warning to the beginning of the video.  Tasting Prototypes  Scenario: a team produces biodegradable food colouring from engineered bacteria. They extract the dye, then make sure that it tastes okay by spreading it on some toast and having a bite.  Rule or Policy violated: Human Experimentation policy (because the toast was eaten by humans), and potentially Release Beyond Containment policy if the dye was brought outside the lab without permission from the Safety & Security Committee  Consequences: The Safety & Security Committee would likely recommend full or partial disqualification of the project. The activity would likely be reported to the host institution as it may be a violation of their rules too. The RCC might also get involved, as such violations also raise questions about whether the team is upholding iGEM’s values.  WHY Questions or Concerns?  To contact the iGEM Safety & Security Committee, please email safety [AT] igem [DOT] org.  To contact the Responsible Conduct Committee, please email rcc [AT] igem [DOT] org.  If you are not sure which committee to contact or if you wish to remain anonymous, you may send an email to iGEM Headquarters at hq [AT] igem [DOT] org for assistance.

Its members come from diverse areas of industry, academia, and government.  The committee helps create iGEM's safety & security program and gives expert advice on potential safety & security issues in the competition.  Responsible Conduct Committee  The iGEM Responsible Conduct Committee (RCC) is an external panel of experts who deal with all issues related to conduct in the competition. Our RCC members collectively have over 50 years of experience in the iGEM competition and are well versed in conduct and behavior related issues.  The role of the Responsible Conduct Committee is to ensure a high standard of conduct on the part of all iGEM participants and to address issues of inappropriate behavior in iGEM. Karmella Haynes is also in the picture, participating virtually. Not pictured: Genya Dana. Rules of Conduct  All members of our community are expected to abide by our Rules of Conduct. These rules apply to everyone involved in iGEM, including the iGEM Competition and League teams (which includes team members, instructors, advisors, and PIs), judges, committee(s) and network members, community participants, and iGEM Headquarters staff.  Failure to follow the Rules of Conduct will be brought to the attention of the Responsible Conduct Committee and they will determine what, if any, action will be taken.  1. Uphold iGEM's Values  Every iGEM participant is expected to uphold iGEM’s values at all times, which include: integrity, good sportsmanship, respect, honesty, celebration, cooperation, effort, and excellence. iGEMers are ambassadors for the global synthetic biology community; teams and projects may have a large impact beyond the competition.  2. Be Intellectually Honest  Teams should describe their accomplishments accurately and honestly. The current year's team members should not take credit for the work of other researchers, even if those researchers were previous members of your institution's iGEM team. This also includes not intentionally misrepresenting results, and not making unsubstantiated claims about your work.  We treat any and all failure to uphold intellectual honesty by anyone associated with a team, including students, advisors, or faculty members, as a form of cheating.  Teams should use the Project Attribution page on their wiki to clearly state who conducted any and all work for the project. If an experiment, tool development, or other part of the project was done by someone who is not currently a member of your team, obtain that person's permission to include their work, and clearly describe their contribution in Project Attribution. If their work was included in a public document or digital medium (publication, website, iGEM Wiki, etc.) clearly cite their work. Teams should also note which parts of the project were derived from the scientific literature throughout their project documentation.  Failure to correctly cite work from others who are not current official team members will be considered a form of plagiarism, which is a form of cheating.  3. Treat Everyone with Respect  All iGEM participants are expected to treat everyone with respect. You must recognize and consider the perspectives, experiences, and dignity of others. You must be sensitive to the inherent worth of all human beings and the consideration that they are due. This includes, but is not limited to, student team members, PIs, instructors, advisors, other teams, judges, community members, Headquarters staff, and members of the public.  4. Consider Cultural Context  We want every member of our community to feel a sense of belonging, and we know that teams (and iGEM HQ) cannot perfectly anticipate what is needed to create a positive shared environment for iGEM’s diverse, global participants. Your online materials and videos may be unintentionally seen as offensive or disrespectful by some members of our community. Equally, you may find materials or videos offensive. In either case, members of our community should consider how cultural contexts differ around the world. When we are notified of these issues, we may ask you to add disclaimers to your materials or revise the content. Hazardous organisms, parts or activities: Teams must submit additional Check-In Forms and get approval by the Safety & Security Committee BEFORE beginning experiments for projects involving parts, organisms, or activities that are not on the White List. Refer to the White List Policy. If considering the use of gene drives within a project, teams will need to refer to the Gene Drives Policy. If planning to use new antimicrobial resistance factors, or those new to a chassis, or their institution, teams will need to refer to the Anti-Microbial Resistance Policy. If intending to use parts from, or live SARS-CoV-2, teams will need to refer to the SARS-CoV-2 Policy. Animal Use Forms: Teams must get permission from the Safety & Security Committee BEFORE beginning experiments for projects involving vertebrates and some invertebrates. This includes the use of live or dead animals, and animal samples such as organs, tissues, blood, saliva, or other bodily fluids. Refer to the Animal Use Policy. Our RCC members collectively have over 50 years of experience in the iGEM competition and are well versed in conduct and behavior related issues.  The role of the Responsible Conduct Committee is to ensure a high standard of conduct on the part of all iGEM participants and to address issues of inappropriate behavior in iGEM.

All members of our community are expected to abide by our Rules of Conduct. These rules apply to everyone involved in iGEM, including the iGEM Competition and League teams (which includes team members, instructors, advisors, and PIs), judges, committee(s) and network members, community participants, and iGEM Headquarters staff.

Every iGEM participant is expected to uphold iGEM’s values at all times, which include: integrity, good sportsmanship, respect, honesty, celebration, cooperation, effort, and excellence. iGEMers are ambassadors for the global synthetic biology community; teams and projects may have a large impact beyond the competition.

We want every member of our community to feel a sense of belonging, and we know that teams (and iGEM HQ) cannot perfectly anticipate what is needed to create a positive shared environment for iGEM’s diverse, global participants. Your online materials and videos may be unintentionally seen as offensive or disrespectful by some members of our community. Equally, you may find materials or videos offensive. In either case, members of our community should consider how cultural contexts differ around the world. When we are notified of these issues, we may ask you to add disclaimers to your materials or revise the content.

Animal Use Forms: Teams must get permission from the Safety & Security Committee BEFORE beginning experiments for projects involving vertebrates and some invertebrates. This includes the use of live or dead animals, and animal samples such as organs, tissues, blood, saliva, or other bodily fluids. Refer to the Animal Use Policy. Failure to meet this requirement has been the most common reason for disqualification of iGEM teams. The team’s Primary PI, Secondary PI, or Instructor must sign the Safety Form and any Animal Use Form the team submits. Teams must meet all safety & security deadlines, including those given in email communications from the Safety & Security Committee. Teams must follow all relevant international, regional, national, local or institutional laws, rules, regulations, or policies, including national or institutional biosafety and biosecurity rules applicable to the each team. For teams conducting any experiment with human subjects (including non-invasive experiments, such as surveys), teams must comply with all rules governing experiments with human subjects. Refer to the Human Experimentation Policy and Human Subjects Research Policy. Teams must work in the biosafety level appropriate for their project. If a project involves organisms and parts that can be used safely in a BSL1 lab, the team should not work at higher containment levels. If this is not possible, an explanation must be provided in the Safety Form. Teams cannot conduct work with Risk Group 3 or 4 organisms, parts from a Risk Group 4 organism, or work in a Safety Level 3 or 4 laboratory. This includes work with large volumes or high concentrations of SARS-CoV-2, whether isolated virus, or human, animal, or environmental samples likely to contain it. Teams cannot release or deploy their project outside of the laboratory at any time during the Competition or at the Grand Jamboree. Refer to the Release Beyond Containment Policy. Teams cannot test their project on or in human subjects. Testing your product on humans (including yourselves) is strictly prohibited. Refer to the Human Experimentation Policy.

Safety Policies provide further clarification on the use of specific technologies in the iGEM Competition. For a more detailed explanation of these policies, and information about how to request permission to use specific technologies, please visit the Safety Policies Introduction. Teams are responsible for checking the Policies page prior to beginning any work, as the policies may be updated throughout the iGEM Competition.

Release Beyond Containment: You cannot release or deploy any genetically modified organisms outside the lab. You must check in before bringing any product of synthetic biology outside of the lab. Review this policy.  White List: You must check in before beginning experiments with any organism, part, or activity that is not on the White List. Review this policy.  Human Experimentation: Testing your project on humans (including yourselves) is strictly prohibited. You must check in before beginning any laboratory experiments involving humans or human samples (including but not limited to blood, DNA, other bodily specimens, and health or psychological outcomes). Review this policy.  Animal Use: You must check in before beginning any experiments involving animals or animal samples. This includes vertebrates (e.g. rats, mice, guinea pigs, hamsters, amphibians, and fishes) and higher order invertebrates (e.g. cuttlefish, octopus, squid, lobster, bees, or American or German cockroaches). Review this policy.  Human Subjects Research: All human subjects research (e.g. surveys, interviews, public engagement) you carry out must be done in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, as well as any institutional rules or guidance. Review this policy.  Gene Drives: Gene drives are not allowed in iGEM projects without a special exception from the Safety & Security Committee. Review this policy.  Antimicrobial Resistance: You must check in before beginning experiments likely to change the risk posed by antimicrobial resistance (e.g. by using novel resistance factors, adding known factors into new organisms, or using resistance factors not previously used in your facility). Review this policy.  SARS-CoV-2: Any work using live SARS-CoV-2 virus (the causative agent of COVID-19) must follow World Health Organization (WHO) guidance, in addition to all local and institutional rules. WHO guidance may be stricter than local safety rules. You must check in before beginning experiments with live SARS-CoV-2 or parts from SARS-CoV-2 . Review this policy.  Environmental Samples: As long as parts or organisms are not isolated from them, samples from the environment, the food industry, or other non-traditional suppliers may be used in your experiments. You must check in before using any parts organisms obtained from outside the lab or from non-traditional suppliers. Review this policy.

These policies are for any material you make as part of your project, including promotional materials, videos, social media posts, wiki pages, and other materials.

Be honest and accurate: You should represent your project and results both honestly and accurately. This is especially important when describing your project's likelihood of solving real world problems. Recognize that many people are eager for hope and it can be tempting to over-promise. An iGEM team is not expected to scale their project into a regional or national solution during one season of the competition. Be yourself: No team member should pretend to have a disability, medical condition, cultural affiliation, or racial identity that they do not have in real life. This may happen with the best of intentions, but comes with a real risk of spreading stereotypes or otherwise failing to treat everyone with respect. No country flags: Country flags are not allowed to be displayed in your videos or promotional materials. We know many teams are proud of the place they come from. However, iGEM is an international competition and we nuture a scientific community of mutual trust and respect, and country flags can unfortunately bring international tensions into what we want to be a collaborative, celebratory environment. Don't include disturbing imagery: We know you may be addressing serious and upsetting issues, but we ask that you consider whether disturbing imagery is truly necessary. Videos containing scenes of violence, death, drug use, or other potentially disturbing content must have warnings added or be removed from iGEM’s platforms. Teams cannot use any copyrighted materials: Copyrighted images and other materials are not permitted on the iGEM wiki. You may use materials that are appropriately licensed for reuse, such as open-source code or Creative Commons licensed images. If you use copyrighted materials, we reserve the right to remove the content at will. Teams must host all online content on iGEM servers: All team pages, images, documents and code must be hosted on the iGEM servers. Load your CSS, Javascript, or Bootstrap files into the iGEM server, either directly into your page or using templates. Do not link to scripts or stylesheets that are hosted on other servers. We preserve all iGEM content on our own servers so future teams can learn from what you have done. When you store content on your own sites or servers, links might become broken, sites might go down, and information will be lost. Hosting content outside of the iGEM servers is a form of cheating and may result in no medal.

The iGEM Foundation strictly prohibits harassment of any kind. For the purposes of this policy, harassment may include, but is not limited to, the following:

any form of verbal, physical, and/or sexual harassment any conduct intended to threaten, intimidate, or coerce another individual uninvited physical contact unwelcome attention intimidation, stalking, or following any discriminatory acts related to age, race, gender, or sexual orientation, status, etc. advocating for or encouraging any of the above behaviors
any conduct intended to threaten, intimidate, or coerce another individual
any discriminatory acts related to age, race, gender, or sexual orientation, status, etc.

Harassment can be verbal or nonverbal, and includes offensive comments and gestures, and the distribution, display, and/or discussion of offensive material. This includes harassment during online events and activities and/or over social media as well as during any in person events.

iGEM Foundation staff will take appropriate and immediate action in response to complaints or knowledge of violations of this policy. During in-person events like the the Grand Jamboree or other iGEM-hosted events, this action may include, but is not limited to, the offender’s immediate ejection from the premises and disqualification of their team from the competition.

Full disqualification: A team is disqualified from the competition. The team is unable to receive any awards or medals, and their wiki may be removed from the iGEM website. Partial disqualification: A part of a team’s project is disqualified. Judges are asked to proceed as if the team had not done that experiment or activity. The team may be asked to edit and/or remove sections of their wiki following the Grand Jamboree. Ineligibility for special prizes: A team is declared ineligible for certain special prizes, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ineligibility for medals: A team is declared ineligible for medals, regardless of the score given to them by judges. Ban from future involvement in iGEM: In the most extreme cases, individuals and/or institutions may be banned from participating in future competitions.

Consequences: When judges learn about these experiments, they ask the Safety & Security Committee whether the team received approval for their animal use work. Since the team did not receive prior approval to use parts of animals, the Safety & Security Committee recommends that the team be disqualified.
Scenario: Some members of a team are unhappy with the judging results and decide to take that frustration out on the judges. They send emails to the judges insulting and threatening them.

Consequences: Consequences could include a team being stripped of awards and individuals banned from future involvement in iGEM. It could also result in an institution being banned from participating in future competitions for a set number of years or indefinitely. In the most extreme cases, matters would be referred to the appropriate legal authorities.

Scenario: A team’s promotional video includes scenes where they pretend to experience a serious medical problem. A judge flags the exaggerated way the team acted out the medical problem, including a scene which shows someone falling into a coma, while a voiceover announces that this condition would not happen if they use the team’s engineered microbiome solution.

Consequences: The RCC reaches out to make sure that the team intended for the video to be respectful, and has engaged responsibly with people who have the medical condition they are portraying during their project. As long as the discussion does not reveal other issues, the only change would be the addition of a content warning to the beginning of the video.

Consequences: The Safety & Security Committee would likely recommend full or partial disqualification of the project. The activity would likely be reported to the host institution as it may be a violation of their rules too. The RCC might also get involved, as such violations also raise questions about whether the team is upholding iGEM’s values.
