iGEM Jamboree Competition More  Sign In  Community Technology Responsibility Startups Leagues Projects On this page Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)  Below we have some of the most frequently asked questions for the iGEM competition. If your question is not answered below, please email us at hq AT igem DOT org and we'll help you!  Team Composition 1. Can one student be a team?  No, iGEM is a team-based program. The interactions of the team members and their advisors are an important part of the iGEM activity. Also, iGEM requires a major effort from the team and it is unlikely that an individual undergraduate student could compete effectively. Finally, the involvement of an instructor is also part of the iGEM program. Simply having a faculty advisor who oversee your work will not be enough. So, find some friends and build a real iGEM team for next year.  2. Can a team have students from more than one school? Can a single school have more than one team?  Yes to both! Many past teams have had students from more than one school, and many schools have had two teams. For example, it is common to have both a traditional-track and a Software track team.  3. How big can a team be?  There is no limit to the number of undergraduate or high-school students on a team, but we recommend 8-15 students per team since this is both a manageable size and also allows teams to accomplish their work. Sometimes, teams do have more than one project. You can also split the team and register two teams.  4. What if our team has students who are 24 years old or older?  The Overgraduate section of iGEM was introduced to allow more people to participate in iGEM. If your team has students who are 24 or older, there are two options:  Students 24 or over can participate as students on your team and the team would compete in the Overgraduate section, or Students 24 or over can participate as advisors or instructors and the team could compete in the Undergraduate section In both scenarios, the team must properly attribute any work done by any and all students in the attributions section of their wikis.  Resources 1. Are there any Discounts and Special Offers offered to iGEM teams?  Yes! iGEM Partner Sponsors have generously provided special offers on products and services designed specifically for iGEM teams. For a complete list of Special offers and Team Grants click here.  Human Practices On Integrated Human Practices 1. What does it mean for Human Practices to be "integrated"?  Your team’s Human Practices work is “integrated” when you go beyond just considering whether your project is responsible and good for the world, but also demonstrate how you respond to your Human Practices reflections, research, and/or engagement. Use the design/build/test/learn cycle of engineering as a model and show us how social feedback or investigation has informed your process.  There are many ways you could respond to your Human Practices, such as:  planning a different application than what you’d originally intended (e.g. Calgary 2019 realizing that synthetic biology could impact every stage of canola production, not just oil processing after stakeholder interviews) updating how end users would interact with your project (e.g. TU Delft 2017 ensuring their diagnostic product could be interpreted with the naked eye) using alternative methods (e.g. deciding to use gene editing techniques rather than recombinant DNA after learning about local regulations on GMOs) choosing a new way to communicate your results (e.g. Marburg 2018 finding ways to express their results for visually-impaired listeners) proposing a regulation or other framework to improve your project’s impact (e.g. suggesting changes to biosecurity DNA screening based on what you learn about non-canonical amino acids)  Any of these responses could be considered “integrating” Human Practices into your project. You can find many more examples on the Projects website. If you’re wondering about the difference between the Human Practices criteria for the Gold and Silver medals, you’ll find related guidance on the Medals page.  2. How important is Integrated Human Practices compared to regular Human Practices?  Integrated Human Practices is just taking your Human Practices work to its logical conclusion, and completing a loop between feedback and project design. When you investigate Human Practices issues related to your project, you should also be asking: what does this mean for how you’re implementing your project? Were you right about who would benefit from your project? Did you discover any concerns about your approach? If you take those questions seriously, and act upon the answers you find, then you will be doing Integrated Human Practices.  3. Do we have to find a stakeholder to tell us what’s wrong with our project?  No. Changing your project based on stakeholder feedback is one way to show you took your Human Practices work seriously, but there are many kinds of Human Practices work that your team could respond to and integrate into your project. In addition to stakeholder engagement, the Exemplary Projects page includes examples of market assessment, policy analysis, ethical explorations, and many other forms of Integrated Human Practices.  Types of work that count as Human Practices 1. Does outreach or educational work count as Human Practices?  Not usually. There are many ways for teams to engage with the public that do not count towards the Human Practices medal requirements, and one of the most common mistakes made by iGEM teams is to classify their public outreach or education activities as Human Practices.  This mistake occurs because outreach activities involve exchanges between your team and the public. However, they do not usually lead to an interchange of ideas between your project and society. To be integrated, your Human Practices work must impact your project’s purpose, design and/or execution.  Although they do not always qualify as Human Practices, education and outreach are important contributions to science in general. To that end, there are special prizes, like the Education prize or the Inclusivity Award, through which your team’s outreach work might be rewarded. These prizes recognize excellent work to establish dialogue with new communities and to engage and involve new people in synthetic biology. You can learn more about these other prizes on the Awards page.  2. My team got advice from a professor at our university about our project– does this count as Human Practices?  We encourage teams to draw from as much expertise as possible in developing their projects. However, part of the goal of Human Practices at iGEM is to encourage teams to engage with issues that extend beyond the lab and even beyond their institution. While seeking expertise from professors may make up a part of your team’s Human Practices effort, we strongly recommend you also seek out input from more diverse communities.  3. If we get feedback on our public engagement work, will that count as Integrated Human Practices?  If the feedback from public engagement affects the purpose, design and/or execution of your project, then it counts as Integrated Human Practices. As one example, the public response to an art exhibit run by your team might raise new ethical or societal issues, causing you to refocus your project. As another example, user feedback on an educational hardware or software tool could cause your team to develop a new way to report your synthetic biology work.  If the feedback does not impact the design or execution of your main project idea, it probably won't count as Integrated Human Practices. However, gathering feedback is still important! It will let you develop better public engagement, will allow you to provide good documentation of your Human Practices methods, and could help your team win special prizes such as Best Education, Best Software Tool, or Best Presentation. You can learn more about these other prizes on the Awards page.  4. My team has an idea for something creative. How do we know if it counts as Human Practices?  Exploring and testing new and creative ideas is something we strongly encourage. We suggest that you take a look at past projects that may have tried similar ideas. If your creative work ties into the design and development of other aspects of your project, it may be considered Integrated Human Practices. If you’re not sure about how to integrate your creative ideas into your project, feel free to contact the Human Practices committee for guidance.  How to do Human Practices 1. Do we need institutional research ethics approval for our Human Practices work?  That depends on your institution. Only your university’s research ethics board (or equivalent research ethics body) has the authority to decide what counts as human subjects research and what requires a human subjects protocol.  Low-risk activities like some direct stakeholder engagements may be exempt from institutional review. Many institutions don’t count informal conversations as “research” unless they are part of a systematic study (such as a survey) or are intended to create publishable, generalized knowledge.  We expect your team to determine which rules apply, to comply with local regulations on research involving human subjects, and to follow valid scientific survey design. You should review the iGEM policy on Human Subjects Research and the sections of the Resources page on informed consent and writing valid surveys.  2. How can my team connect with people or communities related to our project? Where do we start?  You don’t necessarily need to start by connecting with individual people. You can do a background literature review on the societal aspects of your project, just as you will have done for its scientific aspects. Which research teams, especially in the social sciences, have investigated the problem your team is working on?  If you do want to speak with individuals, you might want to start by contacting local businesses or nonprofits that do work related to your project or with experts whose work you’ve come across in your research. Many people will be happy to speak directly to passionate iGEM team members.  When contacting someone, describe who you are and why you’re reaching out to them. Leave short emails or messages with specific questions, so it’s easy for them to respond if they have a tight schedule. Even if they don’t have time to talk, you can ask them to recommend other people for you to contact.  3. Is my team allowed to work on a controversial project? What kind of Human Practices should we do?  A project might be called controversial for many reasons— maybe you think you’re likely to see sensationalist media coverage of your work, maybe your project is connected to hotly-debated ethical issues. These may be the sort of issues that iGEM teams investigate through their Human Practices work. Whether or not your project idea is controversial doesn’t say much about its value.  However, your team will not be rewarded for seeking out controversy, and you should not pursue an idea simply because it’s controversial. Ask yourself whether you’ve found the best approach: are there other ways to solve the same problems? Teams are expected to document the rationale and process by which they select their project. A decision not to use certain methods or pursue certain ideas is a perfectly valid outcome of your Human Practices work, which you can document on your wiki.  If your team decides to go ahead with a controversial project, ensure you treat high-stakes issues with respect. Remember that iGEM students are ambassadors for the global synthetic biology community; what your team does this year may have a large impact beyond the competition. We also recognize that iGEM is an international community, and issues that are contentious and polarizing in one country or culture may already be settled in another.  4. How can my team integrate Human Practices into our Foundational Advance project?  Even projects which aim to develop the technical aspects of synthetic biology, rather than apply them to a real-world problem, can have important societal implications. Some examples of Integrated Human Practices in Foundational Advance projects include Marburg 2018, who integrated what they learned from their engagement with visually-impaired high school students to make both their wiki and presentation accessible, and Heidelberg 2017, who developed software to screen DNA sequences produced by their directed evolution algorithms for any potential safety concerns. Your team could also look into issues of intellectual property, or do stakeholder consultations, with members of the scientific community as stakeholders.  5. What if we want to patent our work?  One of iGEM’s core values is cooperation, which is expressed through the "Get, Give, & Share" philosophy of the Registry of Standard Biological Parts, the open documentation of team wikis, and many other aspects of the competition.  That said, we recognize that your team may wish to secure intellectual property protection for your work, perhaps because, like many iGEM teams before you, you intend to start a company based on your work. Intellectual property law varies greatly between countries, and we encourage you to contact your institution for support in navigating it. Many universities have a Technology Transfer Office- if you have access to one, that's likely a good place to start. You may find the resources offered by the World Intellectual Property Organization, such as country profiles, helpful.  Some previous iGEM teams have documented their thinking about intellectual property. On this page Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)  Below we have some of the most frequently asked questions for the iGEM competition. If your question is not answered below, please email us at hq AT igem DOT org and we'll help you!  Team Composition 1. Can one student be a team?  No, iGEM is a team-based program. The interactions of the team members and their advisors are an important part of the iGEM activity. Also, iGEM requires a major effort from the team and it is unlikely that an individual undergraduate student could compete effectively. Finally, the involvement of an instructor is also part of the iGEM program. Simply having a faculty advisor who oversee your work will not be enough. So, find some friends and build a real iGEM team for next year.  2. Can a team have students from more than one school? Can a single school have more than one team?  Yes to both! Many past teams have had students from more than one school, and many schools have had two teams. For example, it is common to have both a traditional-track and a Software track team.  3. How big can a team be?  There is no limit to the number of undergraduate or high-school students on a team, but we recommend 8-15 students per team since this is both a manageable size and also allows teams to accomplish their work. Sometimes, teams do have more than one project. You can also split the team and register two teams.  4. What if our team has students who are 24 years old or older?  The Overgraduate section of iGEM was introduced to allow more people to participate in iGEM. If your team has students who are 24 or older, there are two options:  Students 24 or over can participate as students on your team and the team would compete in the Overgraduate section, or Students 24 or over can participate as advisors or instructors and the team could compete in the Undergraduate section In both scenarios, the team must properly attribute any work done by any and all students in the attributions section of their wikis.  Resources 1. Are there any Discounts and Special Offers offered to iGEM teams?  Yes! iGEM Partner Sponsors have generously provided special offers on products and services designed specifically for iGEM teams. For a complete list of Special offers and Team Grants click here.  Human Practices On Integrated Human Practices 1. What does it mean for Human Practices to be "integrated"?  Your team’s Human Practices work is “integrated” when you go beyond just considering whether your project is responsible and good for the world, but also demonstrate how you respond to your Human Practices reflections, research, and/or engagement. Use the design/build/test/learn cycle of engineering as a model and show us how social feedback or investigation has informed your process.  There are many ways you could respond to your Human Practices, such as:  planning a different application than what you’d originally intended (e.g. Calgary 2019 realizing that synthetic biology could impact every stage of canola production, not just oil processing after stakeholder interviews) updating how end users would interact with your project (e.g. TU Delft 2017 ensuring their diagnostic product could be interpreted with the naked eye) using alternative methods (e.g. deciding to use gene editing techniques rather than recombinant DNA after learning about local regulations on GMOs) choosing a new way to communicate your results (e.g. Marburg 2018 finding ways to express their results for visually-impaired listeners) proposing a regulation or other framework to improve your project’s impact (e.g. suggesting changes to biosecurity DNA screening based on what you learn about non-canonical amino acids)  Any of these responses could be considered “integrating” Human Practices into your project. You can find many more examples on the Projects website. If you’re wondering about the difference between the Human Practices criteria for the Gold and Silver medals, you’ll find related guidance on the Medals page.  2. How important is Integrated Human Practices compared to regular Human Practices?  Integrated Human Practices is just taking your Human Practices work to its logical conclusion, and completing a loop between feedback and project design. When you investigate Human Practices issues related to your project, you should also be asking: what does this mean for how you’re implementing your project? Were you right about who would benefit from your project? Did you discover any concerns about your approach? If you take those questions seriously, and act upon the answers you find, then you will be doing Integrated Human Practices.  3. Do we have to find a stakeholder to tell us what’s wrong with our project?  No. Changing your project based on stakeholder feedback is one way to show you took your Human Practices work seriously, but there are many kinds of Human Practices work that your team could respond to and integrate into your project. In addition to stakeholder engagement, the Exemplary Projects page includes examples of market assessment, policy analysis, ethical explorations, and many other forms of Integrated Human Practices.  Types of work that count as Human Practices 1. Does outreach or educational work count as Human Practices?  Not usually. There are many ways for teams to engage with the public that do not count towards the Human Practices medal requirements, and one of the most common mistakes made by iGEM teams is to classify their public outreach or education activities as Human Practices.  This mistake occurs because outreach activities involve exchanges between your team and the public. However, they do not usually lead to an interchange of ideas between your project and society. To be integrated, your Human Practices work must impact your project’s purpose, design and/or execution.  Although they do not always qualify as Human Practices, education and outreach are important contributions to science in general. To that end, there are special prizes, like the Education prize or the Inclusivity Award, through which your team’s outreach work might be rewarded. These prizes recognize excellent work to establish dialogue with new communities and to engage and involve new people in synthetic biology. You can learn more about these other prizes on the Awards page.  2. My team got advice from a professor at our university about our project– does this count as Human Practices?  We encourage teams to draw from as much expertise as possible in developing their projects. However, part of the goal of Human Practices at iGEM is to encourage teams to engage with issues that extend beyond the lab and even beyond their institution. While seeking expertise from professors may make up a part of your team’s Human Practices effort, we strongly recommend you also seek out input from more diverse communities.  3. If we get feedback on our public engagement work, will that count as Integrated Human Practices?  If the feedback from public engagement affects the purpose, design and/or execution of your project, then it counts as Integrated Human Practices. As one example, the public response to an art exhibit run by your team might raise new ethical or societal issues, causing you to refocus your project. As another example, user feedback on an educational hardware or software tool could cause your team to develop a new way to report your synthetic biology work.  If the feedback does not impact the design or execution of your main project idea, it probably won't count as Integrated Human Practices. However, gathering feedback is still important! It will let you develop better public engagement, will allow you to provide good documentation of your Human Practices methods, and could help your team win special prizes such as Best Education, Best Software Tool, or Best Presentation. You can learn more about these other prizes on the Awards page.  4. My team has an idea for something creative. How do we know if it counts as Human Practices?  Exploring and testing new and creative ideas is something we strongly encourage. We suggest that you take a look at past projects that may have tried similar ideas. If your creative work ties into the design and development of other aspects of your project, it may be considered Integrated Human Practices. If you’re not sure about how to integrate your creative ideas into your project, feel free to contact the Human Practices committee for guidance.  How to do Human Practices 1. Do we need institutional research ethics approval for our Human Practices work?  That depends on your institution. Only your university’s research ethics board (or equivalent research ethics body) has the authority to decide what counts as human subjects research and what requires a human subjects protocol.  Low-risk activities like some direct stakeholder engagements may be exempt from institutional review. Many institutions don’t count informal conversations as “research” unless they are part of a systematic study (such as a survey) or are intended to create publishable, generalized knowledge.  We expect your team to determine which rules apply, to comply with local regulations on research involving human subjects, and to follow valid scientific survey design. You should review the iGEM policy on Human Subjects Research and the sections of the Resources page on informed consent and writing valid surveys.  2. How can my team connect with people or communities related to our project? Where do we start?  You don’t necessarily need to start by connecting with individual people. You can do a background literature review on the societal aspects of your project, just as you will have done for its scientific aspects. Which research teams, especially in the social sciences, have investigated the problem your team is working on?  If you do want to speak with individuals, you might want to start by contacting local businesses or nonprofits that do work related to your project or with experts whose work you’ve come across in your research. Many people will be happy to speak directly to passionate iGEM team members.  When contacting someone, describe who you are and why you’re reaching out to them. Leave short emails or messages with specific questions, so it’s easy for them to respond if they have a tight schedule. Even if they don’t have time to talk, you can ask them to recommend other people for you to contact.  3. Is my team allowed to work on a controversial project? What kind of Human Practices should we do?  A project might be called controversial for many reasons— maybe you think you’re likely to see sensationalist media coverage of your work, maybe your project is connected to hotly-debated ethical issues. These may be the sort of issues that iGEM teams investigate through their Human Practices work. Whether or not your project idea is controversial doesn’t say much about its value.  However, your team will not be rewarded for seeking out controversy, and you should not pursue an idea simply because it’s controversial. Ask yourself whether you’ve found the best approach: are there other ways to solve the same problems? Teams are expected to document the rationale and process by which they select their project. A decision not to use certain methods or pursue certain ideas is a perfectly valid outcome of your Human Practices work, which you can document on your wiki.  If your team decides to go ahead with a controversial project, ensure you treat high-stakes issues with respect. Remember that iGEM students are ambassadors for the global synthetic biology community; what your team does this year may have a large impact beyond the competition. We also recognize that iGEM is an international community, and issues that are contentious and polarizing in one country or culture may already be settled in another.  4. How can my team integrate Human Practices into our Foundational Advance project?  Even projects which aim to develop the technical aspects of synthetic biology, rather than apply them to a real-world problem, can have important societal implications. Some examples of Integrated Human Practices in Foundational Advance projects include Marburg 2018, who integrated what they learned from their engagement with visually-impaired high school students to make both their wiki and presentation accessible, and Heidelberg 2017, who developed software to screen DNA sequences produced by their directed evolution algorithms for any potential safety concerns. Your team could also look into issues of intellectual property, or do stakeholder consultations, with members of the scientific community as stakeholders.  5. What if we want to patent our work?  One of iGEM’s core values is cooperation, which is expressed through the "Get, Give, & Share" philosophy of the Registry of Standard Biological Parts, the open documentation of team wikis, and many other aspects of the competition.  That said, we recognize that your team may wish to secure intellectual property protection for your work, perhaps because, like many iGEM teams before you, you intend to start a company based on your work. Intellectual property law varies greatly between countries, and we encourage you to contact your institution for support in navigating it. Many universities have a Technology Transfer Office- if you have access to one, that's likely a good place to start. You may find the resources offered by the World Intellectual Property Organization, such as country profiles, helpful.  Some previous iGEM teams have documented their thinking about intellectual property. You can read about the TUDelft 2017 and Stockholm 2018 teams applying for EU patents, and the Manchester 2017 team’s write-up on intellectual property and synthetic biology, which also covers their decision to decide not to pursue a patent.  hq@igem.org + Newsletter iGEM News Visions & Values People Sponsorship Blog Videos Competition Deliverables Calendar Judging iGEM Cycle Starting a Team Projects Team List 2022 Results 2022 Team Presentations 2022 Project Promotions Community Projects News Events Ambassadors SynBio Topics Around the World Technology Registry Distribution Assembly Team Parts Engineering Resources Engineering Webinars Responsibility Safety Policies Human Practices Responsible Design Check In Form Animal Use Form Startups Incubators & Accelerators Venture Foundry Events Startup Showcase Bioinnovation Fair Leagues Design League Indonesian MENA iGEM Academy Jamboree 2023 Grand Jamboree 2022 Grand Jamboree 2022 Photos 2022 Videos 2021 Giant Jamboree 2020 Giant Jamboree iGEM Foundation 45 Prospect Street, 02139 Cambridge MA, USA iGEM Europe 10 rue du Mail, 75002 Paris, France Privacy Policy

Low-risk activities like some direct stakeholder engagements may be exempt from institutional review. Many institutions don’t count informal conversations as “research” unless they are part of a systematic study (such as a survey) or are intended to create publishable, generalized knowledge.  We expect your team to determine which rules apply, to comply with local regulations on research involving human subjects, and to follow valid scientific survey design. You should review the iGEM policy on Human Subjects Research and the sections of the Resources page on informed consent and writing valid surveys.  2. How can my team connect with people or communities related to our project? Where do we start?  You don’t necessarily need to start by connecting with individual people. You can do a background literature review on the societal aspects of your project, just as you will have done for its scientific aspects. Which research teams, especially in the social sciences, have investigated the problem your team is working on?  If you do want to speak with individuals, you might want to start by contacting local businesses or nonprofits that do work related to your project or with experts whose work you’ve come across in your research. Many people will be happy to speak directly to passionate iGEM team members.  When contacting someone, describe who you are and why you’re reaching out to them. Leave short emails or messages with specific questions, so it’s easy for them to respond if they have a tight schedule. Even if they don’t have time to talk, you can ask them to recommend other people for you to contact.  3. Is my team allowed to work on a controversial project? What kind of Human Practices should we do?  A project might be called controversial for many reasons— maybe you think you’re likely to see sensationalist media coverage of your work, maybe your project is connected to hotly-debated ethical issues. These may be the sort of issues that iGEM teams investigate through their Human Practices work. Whether or not your project idea is controversial doesn’t say much about its value.  However, your team will not be rewarded for seeking out controversy, and you should not pursue an idea simply because it’s controversial. Ask yourself whether you’ve found the best approach: are there other ways to solve the same problems? Teams are expected to document the rationale and process by which they select their project. A decision not to use certain methods or pursue certain ideas is a perfectly valid outcome of your Human Practices work, which you can document on your wiki.  If your team decides to go ahead with a controversial project, ensure you treat high-stakes issues with respect. Remember that iGEM students are ambassadors for the global synthetic biology community; what your team does this year may have a large impact beyond the competition. We also recognize that iGEM is an international community, and issues that are contentious and polarizing in one country or culture may already be settled in another.  4. How can my team integrate Human Practices into our Foundational Advance project?  Even projects which aim to develop the technical aspects of synthetic biology, rather than apply them to a real-world problem, can have important societal implications. Some examples of Integrated Human Practices in Foundational Advance projects include Marburg 2018, who integrated what they learned from their engagement with visually-impaired high school students to make both their wiki and presentation accessible, and Heidelberg 2017, who developed software to screen DNA sequences produced by their directed evolution algorithms for any potential safety concerns. Your team could also look into issues of intellectual property, or do stakeholder consultations, with members of the scientific community as stakeholders.  5. What if we want to patent our work?  One of iGEM’s core values is cooperation, which is expressed through the "Get, Give, & Share" philosophy of the Registry of Standard Biological Parts, the open documentation of team wikis, and many other aspects of the competition.  That said, we recognize that your team may wish to secure intellectual property protection for your work, perhaps because, like many iGEM teams before you, you intend to start a company based on your work. Intellectual property law varies greatly between countries, and we encourage you to contact your institution for support in navigating it. Many universities have a Technology Transfer Office- if you have access to one, that's likely a good place to start. You may find the resources offered by the World Intellectual Property Organization, such as country profiles, helpful.  Some previous iGEM teams have documented their thinking about intellectual property. You can read about the TUDelft 2017 and Stockholm 2018 teams applying for EU patents, and the Manchester 2017 team’s write-up on intellectual property and synthetic biology, which also covers their decision to decide not to pursue a patent.
Below we have some of the most frequently asked questions for the iGEM competition. If your question is not answered below, please email us at hq AT igem DOT org and we'll help you!

No, iGEM is a team-based program. The interactions of the team members and their advisors are an important part of the iGEM activity. Also, iGEM requires a major effort from the team and it is unlikely that an individual undergraduate student could compete effectively. Finally, the involvement of an instructor is also part of the iGEM program. Simply having a faculty advisor who oversee your work will not be enough. So, find some friends and build a real iGEM team for next year.

There is no limit to the number of undergraduate or high-school students on a team, but we recommend 8-15 students per team since this is both a manageable size and also allows teams to accomplish their work. Sometimes, teams do have more than one project. You can also split the team and register two teams.

Your team’s Human Practices work is “integrated” when you go beyond just considering whether your project is responsible and good for the world, but also demonstrate how you respond to your Human Practices reflections, research, and/or engagement. Use the design/build/test/learn cycle of engineering as a model and show us how social feedback or investigation has informed your process.

Integrated Human Practices is just taking your Human Practices work to its logical conclusion, and completing a loop between feedback and project design. When you investigate Human Practices issues related to your project, you should also be asking: what does this mean for how you’re implementing your project? Were you right about who would benefit from your project? Did you discover any concerns about your approach? If you take those questions seriously, and act upon the answers you find, then you will be doing Integrated Human Practices.

No. Changing your project based on stakeholder feedback is one way to show you took your Human Practices work seriously, but there are many kinds of Human Practices work that your team could respond to and integrate into your project. In addition to stakeholder engagement, the Exemplary Projects page includes examples of market assessment, policy analysis, ethical explorations, and many other forms of Integrated Human Practices.

Although they do not always qualify as Human Practices, education and outreach are important contributions to science in general. To that end, there are special prizes, like the Education prize or the Inclusivity Award, through which your team’s outreach work might be rewarded. These prizes recognize excellent work to establish dialogue with new communities and to engage and involve new people in synthetic biology. You can learn more about these other prizes on the Awards page.

We encourage teams to draw from as much expertise as possible in developing their projects. However, part of the goal of Human Practices at iGEM is to encourage teams to engage with issues that extend beyond the lab and even beyond their institution. While seeking expertise from professors may make up a part of your team’s Human Practices effort, we strongly recommend you also seek out input from more diverse communities.
3. If we get feedback on our public engagement work, will that count as Integrated Human Practices?

If the feedback from public engagement affects the purpose, design and/or execution of your project, then it counts as Integrated Human Practices. As one example, the public response to an art exhibit run by your team might raise new ethical or societal issues, causing you to refocus your project. As another example, user feedback on an educational hardware or software tool could cause your team to develop a new way to report your synthetic biology work.

If the feedback does not impact the design or execution of your main project idea, it probably won't count as Integrated Human Practices. However, gathering feedback is still important! It will let you develop better public engagement, will allow you to provide good documentation of your Human Practices methods, and could help your team win special prizes such as Best Education, Best Software Tool, or Best Presentation. You can learn more about these other prizes on the Awards page.

Commercial Team Information Form  Each commercial team must submit an additional Team Information Form to iGEM to be approved.  COMMERCIAL TEAM INFORMATION  The button above goes directly to this page: https://competition.igem.org/registration/commercial-teams.  Community Lab Information  Community Labs must contact documents [AT] igem [DOT] org to submit additional Team Information by email. Next Steps  Once your team has submitted the team application, team fee, and relevant consent forms, your information will be sent to iGEM Headquarters (HQ) and we will review it and either accept it, or contact you for more details. All team members may create their user accounts at this stage, but will not be able to join a team roster until this feature is released. We will announce when this is ready via email and the competition homepage.  Information Required to Apply for a Team 1. Team PI Information and Agreement  This PI Information will be automatically filled in on the team application page once the Team PI has logged into their account.  2. Team Name  If your team has participated before, you should use the same team name as previous years. If you are a new team, your team name should be brief and descriptive.  A team name must follow these rules:  must be 20 or fewer characters (including letters, numbers, and hyphen) must only indicate your school name(s), city, state, country, and/or region must contain letters A-Z, and a-z may contain numbers 0-9 may contain hyphen (-) (but NOT underscore (_) ) cannot contain the year (i.e. "24", or "2024") cannot contain spaces (use the hyphen to denote spaces) cannot include the words iGEM, team, or synthetic biology (or any abbreviations, i.e., SynBio) cannot be named after the team's project cannot include the name of your school mascot cannot include sponsor names  Your team name will need to be approved by iGEM HQ. Failure to follow these rules will delay your team approval. If you use any other words besides your school name, city, state, country, or region, we may ask for an explanation for the team name and, depending on the explanation, may suggest alternative names.  Why is your team name important? Your team name is the official name that you will use throughout the entire iGEM season. After the competition ends this name will be used as an historical record of your team. Your team name is your team identity.  3. Team Kind  In iGEM 2024, teams will register as one of four team "kinds":  Collegiate: Student team members are usually collegiate students. You may also have postgraduate students and/or high school students on the team. Collegiate teams compete in all Villages, and in the Undergraduate and Overgraduate Sections based on the team members' ages.  High School: Student team members are only high school students and students who will graduate high school in 2024. High School teams compete with other High School teams in the High School Track and Section. All High School teams must submit additional paperwork to be approved. Please visit the High School Consent Form page for more information.  Community Lab: Student team members are members of a community lab. This can include anyone. Community Lab teams compete with Collegiate teams in all Villages and in the Undergraduate and Overgraduate Sections based on the team members' ages.  Each community lab team must complete the following additional requirements and send the applicable documentation to documents AT igem DOT org:  demonstrate access to a Biosafety Level 1 (BSL-1) lab demonstrate an adequate safety training program must be an incorporated entity (for profit or not-for-profit) must have a legal entity which has the ability to sign contracts  Commercial: These are teams run by companies, including companies contracting to run teams for high schools, colleges, universities, as well as companies recruiting individual members. Commercial teams can include anyone. For this year, ALL teams run by companies MUST register as commercial teams. Commercial teams registering as other kinds (Collegiate, High School, or Community Lab) are NOT be eligible to compete.  For more information about this new kind of iGEM team, including additional registration requirements, please see our Commercial Teams page.  If the Commercial Team is made up of high school students, then the team must submit the Consent Forms as described in the "How to Register" section above.  4. Team Institution/s and Location  Teams are asked to provide their institution/s and location. The team institution refers to the school (college, university, or high school), community lab, or other organization that team participants are affiliated with. If more than one institution is represented on the team, please list each one. You can also add additional schools or organizations after you register the team.  The team PI should be affiliated with the team institution provided at the time of registration.  5. Shipping Information  The shipping information is used to send the team materials during the iGEM 2024 competition season. The Team PI will need the shipping information to finish the team registration application. The shipping address cannot be a personal home address.  Team Requirements  Below are the 2024 team requirements for participating in the iGEM Competition. If you have any questions about these requirements, please email us at hq [AT] igem [DOT] org.  1. Team Composition and Team Roster  iGEM teams consist primarily of undergraduate students at an accredited college or university. Teams may also be composed of postgraduate students, high school students, or community lab members.  Each team has a Team Roster that must be completed by the Team Roster Freeze. The Team Roster must include everyone who is involved with the iGEM team, including professors, teachers, instructors, advisors, and the student team members. This can be an ongoing process as some team members and advisors are added or removed, but we suggest that you fill it as early as possible.  Only team members listed on the Team Roster at the roster freeze will be officially recognized as iGEM Competition participants and receive participation certificates after the Grand Jamboree, so please make sure your Team Roster is correct!  NOTE New iGEM Accounts System  We have migrated to a new system for user accounts (accounts.igem.org) and team registration (teams.igem.org). From January 2024, the previous system (old.igem.org) will no longer be in use.  The new platforms are still in beta release mode. We are actively working on improving them and creating new features for you.  If you have any suggestions or feedback, please don’t hesitate to contact us at hq@igem.org  2. Team Roles  Similar to sports teams, team members have different roles and responsibilities on a team:  Student team member = Team player. Responsible for brainstorming, choosing, and executing project idea Student team leader = Team captain. Primary and Secondary PI = General manager. Individuals in a position of authority Instructor = Head coach. Provides day-to-day support and technical training for the team Advisor = Assistant coach. Provides supplementary support  Role Details  Below are more details for each Team Role. Please read through each role carefully and email us at hq AT igem DOT org with any questions.  Student team member role and requirements  Student team members brainstorm project ideas, choose a project idea, and build and test their chosen biological system. Students are also responsible for documenting their work and for meeting the various iGEM deadlines throughout the iGEM season. Every student team member must do the following by the Team Roster Freeze:  have an iGEM user account enter their age information join the online team roster  Undergraduate and Overgraduate teams have age restrictions for the student team members (see 3. Team Sections below).  Principal investigator (PI) role and requirements  Principal investigators (PIs) are individuals in a position of authority (ex: in a university setting, they are authorized to have lab space, grants, and hiring privileges) who are responsible for the team. This includes the official team registration, the team roster, certifying the safety form, payment of the team’s fees, and any other official aspect of the team. Team PIs provide guidance and support throughout the season, including assistance with fundraising, lab support, and help with school bureaucracy and regulations. PIs should plan on participating in the Grand Jamboree with the team. Team PIs serve as the official points of contact for iGEM Headquarters: they must be able to receive emails and phone calls from iGEM HQ, and respond promptly. Each team must have at least one (1) PI on their team roster at all times throughout the competition.  Each team must have a Primary PI and they must:  have an iGEM user account (this will be required in order to register the team for iGEM 2024) be listed on the Team Roster add the [AT] igem [DOT] org domain to your list of safe contacts to receive emails from iGEM Headquarters staff  Each Team Kind has specific PI requirements:  For Collegiate teams, the primary PI must be a professor. If the team wishes to have more than one PI, the other PIs may be a post-doc or above. For High School teams, the primary PI must be either a principal or teacher. For Community Lab teams, the primary PI must be the director of the community lab. For Commercial teams, the primary PI must be an employee of the company, be authorized to make binding commitments for the company, and be able to authorize the necessary payments.  High School teams and Community Lab teams may have a professor as one of their team PIs if they wish.  We strongly recommend that each team has a Secondary PI, but it is not a requirement. The Secondary PI should serve as a second contact point for the team and should hold the same level of authority for the team as the Primary PI.  Instructor role and requirements  Team instructors provide day-to-day support for the team, and are aware of team activities and experimental plans. Instructors should also be responsible for the technical training of the team members in lab protocols.  Instructors must:  have an iGEM user account join the online team roster by the Team Roster Freeze  Advisor role and requirements  Team advisors include graduate students, post-graduate students, post-docs, and/or technicians who support the team.  Advisors must:  have an iGEM user account join the online team roster by the Team Roster Freeze  3. Team Sections  There are three team sections:  Undergraduate Section: all student team members are age 23 or younger on March 31, 2024. This applies to Collegiate, Community Lab, and Commercial Team Kinds. Overgraduate Section: one or more student team members are older than 23 on March 31, 2024. This applies to Collegiate, Community Lab, and Commercial Team Kinds. High School Section: all student team members are high school students on March 31, 2024; includes students who graduate from high school before July of 2024. This applies to High School and Commercial Team Kinds.  All teams, regardless of their section, have the opportunity to participate in the 2024 Grand Jamboree - it will be the same event for all 3 sections.  ALERT Team Section for Collegiate Teams  For collegiate teams, your team's section will be calculated automatically by the iGEM software based on the ages of the student members on your team roster. Student team member role and requirements  Student team members brainstorm project ideas, choose a project idea, and build and test their chosen biological system. Students are also responsible for documenting their work and for meeting the various iGEM deadlines throughout the iGEM season. Every student team member must do the following by the Team Roster Freeze:  have an iGEM user account enter their age information join the online team roster  Undergraduate and Overgraduate teams have age restrictions for the student team members (see 3. Team Sections below). This includes the official team registration, the team roster, certifying the safety form, payment of the team’s fees, and any other official aspect of the team. Team PIs provide guidance and support throughout the season, including assistance with fundraising, lab support, and help with school bureaucracy and regulations. PIs should plan on participating in the Grand Jamboree with the team. Instructors must:  have an iGEM user account join the online team roster by the Team Roster Freeze  Advisor role and requirements  Team advisors include graduate students, post-graduate students, post-docs, and/or technicians who support the team.  Advisors must:  have an iGEM user account join the online team roster by the Team Roster Freeze  3. Team Sections  There are three team sections:  Undergraduate Section: all student team members are age 23 or younger on March 31, 2024. This applies to Collegiate, Community Lab, and Commercial Team Kinds. Overgraduate Section: one or more student team members are older than 23 on March 31, 2024. This applies to Collegiate, Community Lab, and Commercial Team Kinds. High School Section: all student team members are high school students on March 31, 2024; includes students who graduate from high school before July of 2024. This applies to High School and Commercial Team Kinds.  All teams, regardless of their section, have the opportunity to participate in the 2024 Grand Jamboree - it will be the same event for all 3 sections. Team Roles  Similar to sports teams, team members have different roles and responsibilities on a team:  Student team member = Team player. Responsible for brainstorming, choosing, and executing project idea Student team leader = Team captain. Primary and Secondary PI = General manager. Individuals in a position of authority Instructor = Head coach. Provides day-to-day support and technical training for the team Advisor = Assistant coach. Provides supplementary support  Role Details  Below are more details for each Team Role. Please read through each role carefully and email us at hq AT igem DOT org with any questions.  Student team member role and requirements  Student team members brainstorm project ideas, choose a project idea, and build and test their chosen biological system. Students are also responsible for documenting their work and for meeting the various iGEM deadlines throughout the iGEM season. Every student team member must do the following by the Team Roster Freeze:  have an iGEM user account enter their age information join the online team roster  Undergraduate and Overgraduate teams have age restrictions for the student team members (see 3. Team Sections below).  Principal investigator (PI) role and requirements  Principal investigators (PIs) are individuals in a position of authority (ex: in a university setting, they are authorized to have lab space, grants, and hiring privileges) who are responsible for the team. This includes the official team registration, the team roster, certifying the safety form, payment of the team’s fees, and any other official aspect of the team. Team PIs provide guidance and support throughout the season, including assistance with fundraising, lab support, and help with school bureaucracy and regulations. PIs should plan on participating in the Grand Jamboree with the team. Team PIs serve as the official points of contact for iGEM Headquarters: they must be able to receive emails and phone calls from iGEM HQ, and respond promptly. Each team must have at least one (1) PI on their team roster at all times throughout the competition.  Each team must have a Primary PI and they must:  have an iGEM user account (this will be required in order to register the team for iGEM 2024) be listed on the Team Roster add the [AT] igem [DOT] org domain to your list of safe contacts to receive emails from iGEM Headquarters staff  Each Team Kind has specific PI requirements:  For Collegiate teams, the primary PI must be a professor. If the team wishes to have more than one PI, the other PIs may be a post-doc or above. For High School teams, the primary PI must be either a principal or teacher. For Community Lab teams, the primary PI must be the director of the community lab. For Commercial teams, the primary PI must be an employee of the company, be authorized to make binding commitments for the company, and be able to authorize the necessary payments.  High School teams and Community Lab teams may have a professor as one of their team PIs if they wish.  We strongly recommend that each team has a Secondary PI, but it is not a requirement. The Secondary PI should serve as a second contact point for the team and should hold the same level of authority for the team as the Primary PI.  Instructor role and requirements  Team instructors provide day-to-day support for the team, and are aware of team activities and experimental plans. Instructors should also be responsible for the technical training of the team members in lab protocols.  Instructors must:  have an iGEM user account join the online team roster by the Team Roster Freeze  Advisor role and requirements  Team advisors include graduate students, post-graduate students, post-docs, and/or technicians who support the team.  Advisors must:  have an iGEM user account join the online team roster by the Team Roster Freeze  3. Team Sections  There are three team sections:  Undergraduate Section: all student team members are age 23 or younger on March 31, 2024. This applies to Collegiate, Community Lab, and Commercial Team Kinds. Overgraduate Section: one or more student team members are older than 23 on March 31, 2024. This applies to Collegiate, Community Lab, and Commercial Team Kinds. High School Section: all student team members are high school students on March 31, 2024; includes students who graduate from high school before July of 2024. This applies to High School and Commercial Team Kinds.  All teams, regardless of their section, have the opportunity to participate in the 2024 Grand Jamboree - it will be the same event for all 3 sections.  ALERT Team Section for Collegiate Teams  For collegiate teams, your team's section will be calculated automatically by the iGEM software based on the ages of the student members on your team roster. Be sure to include ages for all student team members, otherwise the system will default to placing your team in the Overgraduate section even if you are an Undergraduate team.

The new platforms are still in beta release mode and we are actively working on improving them and creating new features for you. If you have any suggestions or feedback, please don’t hesitate to contact us at hq@igem.org.  Fees Competition Program Team Fees  All teams must pay the Competition Program Fee to register for the iGEM Competition. Registration is subject to Terms and Conditions.  Please Note: This does NOT include registration for the Grand Jamboree event. The Grand Jamboree has a separate event registration period later in the year (see the next section below).  Registration Cost Payment Deadline  Early Competition Program Fee   $5500 USD February 23, 2024 19:00 (+04)   Regular Competition Program Fee   $6000 USD April 5, 2024 18:00 (+04)   Late Competition Program Fee   $6500 USD May 22, 2024 18:00 (+04) Grand Jamboree Registration  The Team Grand Jamboree fee is $3000 USD and secures your team’s Judging Session at the Grand Jamboree. The Judging Session assignment makes your team eligible for medals and prizes. Every team must pay this fee by July 31, 2024 18:00 (+04) to participate in the Grand Jamboree. Registrations are now open and can be submitted here.  Note: Team members who wish to attend the Paris Jamboree in person must also purchase a separate ticket to the event.  Team Member Tickets  All team members who wish to attend the Grand Jamboree in Paris must purchase a Team Member Ticket which is from $550 USD per person. Payment Instructions  To submit a payment, the Team PI must generate an order using iGEM's payment platform.  START A PAYMENT!  Go to payments.igem.org  Log in (Team PI only)  Create an order and add items to cart  Add your billing address, and select it once added  Select the team you would like to apply the payment to  Click "Create Order"  From here, you can generate an invoice, submit credit card payments, get instructions to do a wire transfer or pay by check. Once you have generated the order, you can share the invoice with the person responsible for making payments at your institution.  Visit payments.igem.org at any time to see payment status.  If you have multiple teams, you will need to generate one order (and invoice) per team.  Partial Payments You are allowed to submit half payments. This can be done in two equal installments by credit card, wire transfer or one of each. Supplementary Information After making a wire transfer, please make sure to upload a transfer confirmation on your payment page on payments.igem.org. When making a wire transfer, please request that all fees (from both the sending and receiving banks) be paid by your account. Please be aware that you are responsible for the payment for all of the requested items and all bank fees. If the wired funds are insufficient, you will be invoiced for the difference and are liable for that payment. All funds should be in US dollars. Be sure to allow enough time (5-10 days) for the transfer to arrive by the payment deadline. The United States does not participate in IBAN. Therefore, US banks do not have an IBAN number. Refund Policy  Refunds will be made in US dollars and processed in the manner in which they were received with the possible exception of wire payments which, at the organizers' discretion, may be refunded via check. If a refund is made via wire transfer, any bank fees will be deducted from the refund. iGEM is not responsible for cancellations or the inability of a team to participate due to weather, threat of terrorism, act of God and other events beyond iGEM's control. Read the Competition terms and conditions here. Please see individual refund conditions below:  Program registration: In order to qualify for a refund of your team registration fee, team registration cancellation requests must be sent in writing to hq AT igem DOT org by April 5, 2024 18:00 (+04). All refunds are subject to a $300 USD cancellation fee and the conditions stated above. Team Grand Jamboree registration: In order to qualify for a refund of your Grand Jamboree team registration fee, cancellation requests must be sent in writing to hq AT igem DOT org by July 31, 2024 18:00 (+04). All refunds are subject to a $200 USD cancellation fee and the conditions stated above. Individual Grand Jamboree tickets: In order to qualify for a refund of your Team Member, Student, Non-Profit/Government/Academic or Corporate/Industry ticket fee, cancellation requests must be sent in writing to hq AT igem DOT org by September 24, 2024 18:00 (+04). All refunds are subject to a $50 USD cancellation fee and the conditions stated above. Payment requests by email  Invoices are now automated through the new payment system. However, if iGEM should ever need to manually issue an invoice, you will only receive an official iGEM invoice from either Lucas Boldrini (lucas AT igem DOT org) or Sarah Beguelin (sarah AT igem DOT org). Please check the sender email address before opening the invoice. If you receive an invoice or message from any other address asking for payment, do not trust the message and contact us immediately. iGEM Jamboree Competition More Community Technology Responsibility Startups Leagues Projects On this page ANNOUNCEMENT 2024 Competition Registration now open! Principal Investigators We love our PIs! Thank you for serving  Principal Investigators (PIs) play an important role on the iGEM team. PIs are individuals in a position of authority who are responsible for the iGEM team. Team PIs provide guidance and support throughout the season, including assistance with fundraising, lab support, and help with school bureaucracy and regulations. PIs should also plan on participating in the Grand Jamboree with the team.  As the iGEM Competition continues to expand each year, we want to reaffirm the essential roles that each PI plays. For example, without a PI, a team cannot:  Register their Team for the Competition Submit the team registration fee Edit the Team Roster Submit the Project Safety Form  Furthermore, team PIs also serve as the official points of contact for the team: If anything happens with the team, iGEM HQ will try to contact the Team PI first. If the PI is not available then that’s when delays can happen and critical deadlines could be missed.  Successful iGEM teams have committed PIs. To codify these roles and responsibilities across the community, we are asking PIs to affirm their commitment by agreeing to a standard set of terms during the Team Application. If you have already registered your team, then you have already agreed.  Your participation in iGEM as a PI also implies your agreement with these roles and responsibilities. If you have not seen the language, but you are a team PI then you can look below for a copy of the agreement. If you still have questions about your role as a PI, please reach out to us at hq [AT] igem [DOT] org.  Thank you for guiding and inspiring another cohort of young synthetic biologists!  PI Agreement Language  Please see below for the language of the new PI Agreement.  *This is different from consent forms.  PINNED   The PI is responsible for the safety of each participant. The PI understands that participation in the iGEM program may expose student members on the official Team Roster to biological laboratory procedures and protocols. The PI understands that iGEM does not select, employ, supervise or otherwise exercise authority or control over the teachers, mentors, and other participants in iGEM projects and programs. The PI acknowledges and agrees that the PI is primarily responsible for team member safety and that the PI will monitor each participant’s participation in the iGEM program.  Team Roster Requirements: For all teams except High School Section teams: The PI is responsible for listing participants on the official Team Roster. The Primary PI and Secondary PI, if applicable, are the only people who can add or remove participants from the official iGEM Team Roster. The Primary PI and/or Secondary PI have until the published date of the Roster Freeze deadline to add or remove individuals from the official iGEM Team Roster. The PI understands that only individuals listed on the official iGEM Team Roster by the published Roster Freeze deadline will be recognized as participants in iGEM for the applicable season. For High School Section Teams: PIs of High School Section teams are reminded that a team member is not fully accepted until each team member (or their Parent/Guardian for those under age 18) has properly submitted a consent form. We encourage PIs to monitor the official Team Roster throughout the season to determine that each member is eligible. If you are working at a lab outside your institution, the PI is responsible for getting permission from the head of department at that institution.  *If a team changes their PI mid-season, the new PI agrees that these conditions apply.  **Each Team Kind has specific PI requirements. Thank you for serving  Principal Investigators (PIs) play an important role on the iGEM team. PIs are individuals in a position of authority who are responsible for the iGEM team. Team PIs provide guidance and support throughout the season, including assistance with fundraising, lab support, and help with school bureaucracy and regulations. PIs should also plan on participating in the Grand Jamboree with the team.  As the iGEM Competition continues to expand each year, we want to reaffirm the essential roles that each PI plays. For example, without a PI, a team cannot:  Register their Team for the Competition Submit the team registration fee Edit the Team Roster Submit the Project Safety Form  Furthermore, team PIs also serve as the official points of contact for the team: If anything happens with the team, iGEM HQ will try to contact the Team PI first. If the PI is not available then that’s when delays can happen and critical deadlines could be missed.  Successful iGEM teams have committed PIs. To codify these roles and responsibilities across the community, we are asking PIs to affirm their commitment by agreeing to a standard set of terms during the Team Application. If you have already registered your team, then you have already agreed.  Your participation in iGEM as a PI also implies your agreement with these roles and responsibilities. If you have not seen the language, but you are a team PI then you can look below for a copy of the agreement. If you still have questions about your role as a PI, please reach out to us at hq [AT] igem [DOT] org.  Thank you for guiding and inspiring another cohort of young synthetic biologists!  PI Agreement Language  Please see below for the language of the new PI Agreement.  *This is different from consent forms.  PINNED   The PI is responsible for the safety of each participant. The PI understands that participation in the iGEM program may expose student members on the official Team Roster to biological laboratory procedures and protocols. The PI understands that iGEM does not select, employ, supervise or otherwise exercise authority or control over the teachers, mentors, and other participants in iGEM projects and programs. The PI acknowledges and agrees that the PI is primarily responsible for team member safety and that the PI will monitor each participant’s participation in the iGEM program.  Team Roster Requirements: For all teams except High School Section teams: The PI is responsible for listing participants on the official Team Roster. The Primary PI and Secondary PI, if applicable, are the only people who can add or remove participants from the official iGEM Team Roster. The Primary PI and/or Secondary PI have until the published date of the Roster Freeze deadline to add or remove individuals from the official iGEM Team Roster. The PI understands that only individuals listed on the official iGEM Team Roster by the published Roster Freeze deadline will be recognized as participants in iGEM for the applicable season. For High School Section Teams: PIs of High School Section teams are reminded that a team member is not fully accepted until each team member (or their Parent/Guardian for those under age 18) has properly submitted a consent form. We encourage PIs to monitor the official Team Roster throughout the season to determine that each member is eligible. If you are working at a lab outside your institution, the PI is responsible for getting permission from the head of department at that institution.  *If a team changes their PI mid-season, the new PI agrees that these conditions apply.  **Each Team Kind has specific PI requirements. Please see the PI section of the Team Requirements for more details about who can be a PI.

Consent Forms  In addition to the general team registration requirements, each high school team must complete and submit a set of consent forms. This also includes Commercial Teams and Community Lab Teams that are comprised of high school students. Consent forms are required from all high school team participants including instructors, advisors, students, and others. We must receive a consent form for each team member in order to approve his/her iGEM.org user account.  Which consent forms are required? Consent Forms Required for Team Registration  Teams must submit the following consent forms during registration to be approved:  Principal consent form for every school represented on the team (This does not apply to Commercial Teams) Participant consent form from the primary PI of the team  A team must submit their consent forms using the online consent form system below. If you cannot access the online system, please contact us for an alternative method for submitting the consent forms.  Consent Forms Required to Join Team Roster  All High School participants must submit the following consent form to be added to the team roster, and gain access to the team wiki and iGEM Registry:  Participant Consent Form - One per student team member, advisor, instructor, and secondary PI (if applicable). REMINDER Deadline  All the required consent forms must be submitted by July 17, 2024 18:00 (+04).  Online Consent Form System ANNOUNCEMENT Team Rosters are ready to join!  Team rosters have been migrated to the new system on teams.igem.org, and are now ready for joining!  Be sure to create an iGEM.org user account first. The online consent form will request your iGEM.org username, official Team Name, and Team ID. The Team Name and Team ID can be found on your Team Information page. You may access the online consent form system using the appropriate links below. After completing the form, you will receive a verification email from SmartWaiver. You will need to click on the link in the email verification in order to complete the process. Be sure to check both your inbox and spam box for this email.  Please note that consent forms will be manually checked by iGEM HQ staff, and it may take longer than you expect for your status to be updated in your Team Information page. If there are errors in your consent form (e.g. participant or team name does not match our database) you may be contacted by us to submit a new form, which will add to the processing time.  Note: Your team name must be approved by iGEM Headquarters BEFORE you submit your consent forms, as the team name on the consent form must match your approved team name. If you submit your form before your team name is approved, you may be asked to re-submit your consent forms.  All teams must complete and submit the following consent forms:  Principal Consent Form  Each school represented on the team must submit a principal consent form. This form is a confirmation that the school is aware of the team's participation in iGEM. Note: your principal does not need an iGEM.org user account in order to access or complete the consent form.  PRINCIPAL CONSENT FORM  Note: This does not apply to Commercial Teams  Participant Consent Form  Every team member (PI, instructor, student, advisor, etc.) must complete a participant consent form. Create your iGEM.org user account first, then click on the button to complete your consent form. The consent form will ask for your iGEM.org username and associated email address. Students: if you are under the age of 18, your parent/guardian will need to submit a signature. Submit your form as soon as possible so we can approve your iGEM.org user account, and you can gain access to the Registry as well as your team wiki!  PARTICIPANT CONSENT FORM NOTE Questions? Commercial Teams Quick Links  CTOE Application Fee Payment  CTOE Application Form  Commercial Team Information Form  Several years ago, iGEM became aware that some teams began to be organized not by schools but by third-party institutions. These third-party institutions were building and organizing teams for schools that did not have access to laboratory facilities and/or for high school students who did not have an iGEM program at their own school. These third-party institutions provided access to iGEM for participants and schools that otherwise did not have such opportunities but iGEM recognized they are organized differently than traditional iGEM teams.  To best accommodate this alternative team format in the iGEM competition, iGEM has been experimenting with a new team called “commercial teams” since 2021. In the past 3 years, we witnessed that student members of commercial teams surprised us by how much they were able to excel within an iGEM season. The results can be attributed to their dedicated work, diversity of the team composition and the additional support and resources provided by the commercial team organizers.  As we have learned more about the commercial team phenomenon, we observed that the variation of how iGEM teams are run across the commercial team organizers is more diverse and complicated than we expected. To continue the experiment of commercial teams in iGEM, we need to increase our understanding of these teams and their processes. In 2023, we introduced the new registration requirements for commercial teams. These requirements will help to ensure all the iGEM teams, despite their team kind, are participating in the competition in a transparent and responsible way, respecting and complying with iGEM's Values and Rules.  NOTE  ALL teams run by companies MUST register as commercial teams. Commercial teams registering as other kinds (Collegiate, High School, or Community Lab) are NOT eligible to compete. This includes companies that:  Offer services to high schools, colleges, universities or other institutions and help to run their teams Recruit individual members from different institutions (such as high schools, or colleges or universities)  ALERT  Competition eligibility can be revoked at any time before, during, or after the Jamboree at the discretion of iGEM. To ensure all iGEM participants can compete and get credit for their work, we highly encourage teams to register as the appropriate team kind when they first sign up.  Registration Process for Commercial Teams in 2024 Apply To Be a Commercial Team Organizing Entity (CTOE)  To be an eligible Commercial Team Organizing Entity, companies MUST submit the Commercial Team Organizing Entity (CTOE) Application Form and agree with the commercial team iGEM participation terms.  PINNED  The application process for CTOEs imposes additional administrative tasks on iGEM HQ to review the commercial team variation and ensure fairplay across the iGEM competition.  To support this process, a one-time fee of $5000 will be required at the time of application.  The application fee is not refundable, even if the application is revoked by the applicant or rejected by iGEM. Please kindly note that the completion of the application process including the payment does not guarantee approval.  Once an application and payment are submitted successfully, we will start the review process. It is possible that iGEM HQ may contact the applicant for more materials or information during the review process. Please feel free to contact commercial-teams [AT] igem [DOT] org if you have any questions regarding this application process. We are eager to help the prospective CTOEs understand the required information and materials for the application process.  Register All Commercial Teams  The Primary PI of each team must be an employee of the CTOE, be authorized to make binding commitments for the company and be able to authorize the necessary payments for each team’s participation in the iGEM Competition.  To register a commercial team, the Commercial Team Organizing Entity will need to do two things:   Register as an iGEM 2024 Team.  Complete a Commercial Team Information Form for each team. We require the Commercial Team Information form for every team because we understand that even if run by the same organizer, teams may work differently and receive support from different external collaborators of the company.  Registering as a Commercial team will NOT impact the experience of team members. Teams that consist of only high school students will continue to compete against other High School teams as part of the High School Track. Teams with collegiate students will compete against other Collegiate teams in the other Tracks and in the Undergraduate and Overgraduate Sections based on the team members' ages.  REMINDER Register Your Commercial Teams  Please note, the teams will not be accepted before your application of becoming a Commercial Team Organizing Entity gets approved by iGEM HQ.
